subtopic: MEDICARE-IMPLEMENTATION IN FORM AND AT DATE ORIGINALLY PLANNED

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: MEDICARE-IMPLEMENTATION IN FORM AND AT DATE ORIGINALLY PLANNED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will undoubtedly recall that last July at the federal-provincial conference the Prime Minister stated that the federal government would be prepared to make contributions to provinces with respect to medical care programs if such programs met four principles established by the federal government. The hope was expressed at that time that a commencement date of July 1, 1967 would be found to be practicable.
Subsequently, at a meeting of ministers of health held early this year in Ottawa, it was announced in the final communique that several provinces had accepted the federal medical care proposals and had indicated their readiness to commence programs by July 1, 1967. Certain provinces, however, were unprepared to make definite commitments at that time. Nevertheless it was made clear that the objective of the federal government was to commence to make contributions on a nation-wide basis by the target date.
During recent weeks there have been further indications of readiness to proceed on the part of other provinces, through statements made in provincial legislatures. Questions have been raised in this house as to whether the federal government would proceed as from the target date regardless of the
number of provinces committed to participate.
In order to make the position of the federal government quite clear in this regard, and to enable the provinces to plan in an orderly way in advance of the commencement date, I should like to state that the federal government proposes to proceed with the medical care program in the form, and from the date, originally planned. It is proposed to introduce the necessary legislation to enable the federal government to make contributions to any province having a program in operation on July 1, 1967 which meets the four established principles, irrespective of the number of provincial governments having such programs in operation at that time.

subtopic: MEDICARE-IMPLEMENTATION IN FORM AND AT DATE ORIGINALLY PLANNED
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MEDICARE-IMPLEMENTATION IN FORM AND AT DATE ORIGINALLY PLANNED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a word to express a very warm welcome for the statement the Minister of National Health and Welfare has just made to the house. The statement is so welcome that I shall not make any comment about how long we have been waiting for it.
We approve of the four conditions which the government laid down when it got into business in this field, namely the coverage of most kinds of medical care, universality as far as people are concerned, all plans to be government operated, and each plan to be fully portable. The one weakness in the government's position until a few weeks or a few months ago was that the government seemed to be waiting for all or most of the provinces to indicate their willingness to come in. The announcement today that the government is prepared to bring forward this legislation and let it come into effect in any of those provinces which are prepared to co-operate constitutes a signal and important statement.
We believe that if the government will bring this legislation before parliament at an early date it will find this house ready to co-operate in order to get the measure through so that we can at last take this important step in social legislation.

maintopic: FINANCE-TIGHT MONEY POLICY-NEGATIVE APPROACH TO PROBLEMS
FINANCE-TIGHT MONEY POLICY-NEGATIVE APPROACH TO PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now witnessing a novel situation where the official opposition has brought in an amendment to a supply motion-and the three members on the government side who have so far spoken in the debate have all admitted that there were problems in housing in Canada. I hope tonight these gentlemen will vote for the amendment, they having realized that there is a problem which must be cured in the immediate future.
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Northumberland deals with the tight money policy of the government, how it is affecting the economy of the country and housing in particular. The amendment relates to the existence of this tight money policy and the economic ills which have brought it about. The tight money policy of today has been caused by the financial blunder of the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance.
May 17, 1966

No one speaks today of an inflation psychosis. It is real, and it is with us. As I have said, the financial blunder of the budget is the cause of this inflation. It has been brought about through the indecision of the government in monetary matters and in not using effectively the monetary machinery and techniques available to the government to check the continual decline in the value of the dollar which, if left unchecked, could lead us to the brink of bankruptcy.
I said on a previous occasion that the approach of the Minister of Finance to inflationary problems in this nation today has been negative. It has completely ignored the increase in productivity; has discouraged the expansion of production in this country; has withheld certain projects which could contribute to an expanded production; and has allowed the reduction of our productive capacities across the country. This was the negative approach taken by the government. I believe, Mr. Speaker, everyone will admit that the only possible solution to this inflationary pressure in Canada is to increase productivity.
A growing economy needs a growing supply of money, thus assuring a fairly steady growth curve. A full economy requires the full employment of our human and material resources. This is not the approach taken by those who sit on the treasury benches. They believe in a tight money policy similar to that of 1956, which opened the door to recession and retarded economic growth. Shortage of funds is not the responsibility of the banks, the insurance companies or other lending institutions. Shortage of money is the outcome of the policies of the government of the day.
If the government is sincerely in favour of tight money to fight inflation, then why does it not explain its policy to the people? It hates to face up to or discuss the problem, hiding behind the blame which is placed on the banks and the other financial institutions of this country. This is unfair to the banks and is creating a superficial inflation additional to an already existing and real one.
It is well known that tight money comes about when the Bank of Canada decreases the cash reserves of the banks or holds them constant, when growing demands exist from bank customers for more loans. The end result is that money and credit grows scarcer and inevitably dearer. The long delay in the revision of the Bank Act is the largest single 23033-3311
Tight Money Policy
contributor to the fact that today there exists in this country a tight money policy.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Since 1963 we have been speaking about bringing in revisions to the Bank Act. That, to date, has not been done, with the end result that today banks, and other lending institutions do not care over much to place their money in the mortgage field. Those institutions possibly are carrying larger cash reserves than are necessary. I believe the financial institutions want to know what will happen to them after the Bank Act is revised. Passage of this measure will greatly relieve the money supply situation. Only then will people be able to get money for house building and for urban development.
I therefore urge the government to pass this legislation as soon as possible, thereby allowing banks and lending institutions to know the conditions under which they will operate for the next ten years.
The tight money policy is affecting those who today need housing. It is also affecting the small businessmen of our country. They are the ones caught in the squeeze. In most cases they deal with consumers and if the consumers, pressed by inflation and additional living costs, cannot make ends meet, cannot look after their own material welfare, how can they pay their bills? As a result the businessman is caught in the financial squeeze, and because of the tight money policy cannot borrow more money from the lending institutions. As a result he cannot expand, and in some cases has to retrench his position because he is not paid for his products.
I am convinced that by increasing national productivity; by making more goods available and making inventories reasonably sufficient to meet daily requirements is one way of meeting inflationary pressures. However, that is not the only way to cure inflation.
I strongly urge the government to take another look at its fiscal policies, with a view to possibly changing them in order to relieve the country of the inflationary danger which now faces it. An economy to keep growing requires full employment of human and material resources. We are neglecting those whose fate it is the hardest to solve; those now living in pockets of high unemployment and poor productivity.

May 17, 1966
Tight Money Policy
We must also realize that to combat inflation and the causes of tight money the government should retrench with respect to federal expenditures. I agree with this move which the government has tentatively made. However, I think it should have gone further and retrenched in expenditures on projects which by their nature are unproductive. It should have concentrated on projects in areas of high unemployment, which could have been a contributing factor to increased national productivity. That indirectly would have raised the standards of living of those who still aspire to reach the average national income.
Insurance companies and large lending institutions are in an unsecure position. They have a greater proportion of liquid assets on hand than is necessary. This is because they are awaiting the amendment to the Bank Act.
Yesterday we heard many hon. members speaking about the needs for additional housing in this country. I do not think it would be unrealistic to state that in 1966 we need not 160,000, not 170,000 dwellings, but 190,000 dwellings. Statistics will show that people now coming into the labour force, that estimated 1 million people for whom we shall have to find jobs in the near future, all aspire to having a home. It is regrettable to note that we shall build fewer homes this year than we did last year, when we ought to be building 5 per cent to 10 per cent more. Two billion dollars will be needed for mortgage financing in 1966. I hope this money will be made available, either by direct government lending or by informing lending institutions of how they will be affected by the new Bank Act, thereby possibly bringing about a release of money for the home building industry.
I am not sure whether the government is delaying construction during the summer . months in order to allow more building to take place during the winter months when unemployment is higher. I would, however, utter a word of caution. In certain areas of Canada it is practically impossible to build a home in the winter as cheaply as in the summer. Many of those who were promised the $500 bonus for building during the winter months to date cannot obtain their money; not because they have not completed their houses inside; not because the houses are uninhabited, but in five cases that I personally know of because houses could not be completed owing to the rigours of the winter. I hope the minister realizes that finishing bricks, mortar and other exterior parts of

houses is difficult when those building the houses face temperatures of 10, 15 or even 20 degrees below zero.
Possibly I should not neglect at this time to thank the Minister of Labour for having opened an office in the lower St. Lawrence region. That will permit prospective home builders to obtain advice and to meet at first hand the employees of the office, thereby facilitating ways and means by which funds can be obtained. I hope that opening the office does not mean that no more money is available for the lower St. Lawrence; I trust there will be funds left over for those in that region who wish to borrow.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
One of the dangers of curtailing the housing program is the possible loss of our skilled labour force. The president of the National Housebuilders' Association, Mr. Gelinas, is accusing the government of having pushed house prices beyond the means of many Canadians. He also states that last year the federal government asked the industry to gear itself in readiness to double production. Obviously such planning needs an assurance that mortgage money will be available. Mr. Gelinas is reported in the Globe and Mail of April 7 as saying:
Today the government, in its concern about inflation, has taken a deliberate course to restrict mortgage funds available under the National Housing Act. Our members have already experienced the apparent new policy which has even removed Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation from its normal role as a lender of last resort.
In some areas it appears that the corporation has declined to approve loans for presold houses to home-owner applicants. Mr. Gelinas comments:
It is our contention that this policy is not halting inflationary trends, but rather is contributing to inflation.
When a man with the authority and experience of Mr. Gelinas speaks on this subject everyone must recognize that there is a danger attached to the restriction of the housing program. I believe that the tight money policy, if unchanged, will lead to economic disaster in those areas of Canada where there is at present a depression or where unemployment figures are high. People living in such areas never seem to reach a fair goal. When times are good across the country we bring in a tight money policy. We say there are inflationary pressures in the economy and proceed to carry out measures of retrenchment.
May 17, 1966

On the other hand, during a period of recession we tend to bring in policies beneficial to areas which have shared most in the good times and the other people to whom I have referred are left to suffer their fate. I sincerely urge the government to take a second look at those of its policies which have helped to create inflation and to introduce others designed to remove inflation as quickly as possible. They should not allow their present policies to prolong the inflationary pressures now present in our economy and which must be eradicated if we are to bring a fair degree of prosperity to our citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was somewhat surprised when I read the motion of censure moved by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) to see that the government is blamed for restricting loans made by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
People seem to think that the C.M.H.C. is a lending company which must loan money to the contractors who want to expand their industry.
Such is not my opinion because the C.M.H.C. exists only to stimulate the private sector of the building industry. I would like to quote from a booklet published by the C.M.H.C. about some of the responsibilities of that corporation which is not, in my opinion, a lending company:
As a result, the corporation is concerned with all the aspects of housing, of the expansion and development of cities. In addition to looking after mortgage loans, the corporation is concerned with research on housing, city planning and urban renewal, with the creation and expansion of the mortgage market, with the improvement of house plans and building as well as with the construction of houses to meet the needs of some particular groups, such as old people, low-income families and university students.
That is the framework within which I will discuss this afternoon the motion of censure before the house.
People seem shocked because the government is limiting borrowing sources. In a statement made last May 3, the responsible minister said:
-the government is taking, and will continue to take every step necessary to ensure a program of direct mortgage loans by Central Mortgage and Housing at the same level as that of last year when, including the fall program, loans for approximately 31,500 houses were approved-
Tight Money Policy
There is no restriction. The government is undertaking today to continue the same expansion program in the housing field as last year.
The government does not refuse to guarantee loans. It is up to private industry to find lending companies which will enable it to continue its work.
Personally, since I represent a riding in the city of Montreal, I will limit my remarks to urban renewal in connection with the construction of one-family dwellings.
In Montreal now the problem is as follows: a part of the population is leaving to settle in the suburbs. The same thing is happening in most of the large cities, and that is why there are houses to rent. They are vacant because it is impossible to offer the citizens modern and sanitary housing such as they can get in the suburbs.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
I have friends of my own who bought houses in the suburbs and, within a year, they were obliged to come back to live in the city of Montreal for the school boards of certain suburbs could not provide the facilities available in the metropolis. Some families must therefore come back to the big city of Montreal, where they have all the required facilities.
I do want to discuss urban renewal, because I five with this problem in the city of Montreal. I have referred to this problem on many occasions in this house, and, in my capacity as a member for 16 years of the Montreal municipal council, I shall continue to advocate urban renewal.
I am very pleased that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act was amended in 1964, precisely to facilitate these renewal developments.
The problem faced by our municipalities in the province of Quebec is that the provincial government did not always take a hard look at this problem. In all other provinces, the authorities have set up a municipal board, tp provide the various municipalities with the facilities to consider the renewal problem. That is what we lacked in the province of Quebec.
The city of Montreal succeeded, in the past, in developing the housing centre known as "Les habitations Jeanne-Mance". The only outlay by the provincial government was a $1 million grant, and had it not been for the good will of the municipal administration at

May 17, 1966
Tight Money Policy
the time, which concentrated its work toward the improvement of the centre, "Les habitations Jeanne-Mance" would not exist today.
Since then, we have had two large sections expropriated for renewal in Montreal, that is the C.B.C. section and Victoriatown, which were torn down for improvement; but no other area was restored since the construction of "Les habitations Jeanne-Mance" in Montreal.
Even if the situation requires it, no other project is being developed at this time. But a 263-acre project called 'La Petite Bourgogne" will shortly be started, in my constituency. This 263-acre area is going to be a most difficult problem for the city of Montreal, because the province of Quebec organized the General Housing Corporation only a year ago. That body is still surveying the problems and cannot, at this time, assist in any way the municipalities which would call on its services. I hope that the government will shortly take the necessary steps to help it show what it is worth.
The evil of slums is not simply an almost latent sore but a grave illness affecting a large part of the social body of which we are all limbs. Those who have had to live in those slum areas know what it means. Unfortunately, members who live in areas where construction is largely of the detached unit type are not aware of the problems involved in renewal. It would surely be proper if every member were informed of this problem. Before lending money for the construction of single family units, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should- and will-contribute to further promotion of the renewal plan. I understand that the C.M.H.C. can do nothing unless the provincial government helps the municipalities in these areas.
The first responsibility for a building lies of necessity with the owner who must protect his building against wear and tear, make it pleasant and clean and modernize it. The tenant also has some responsibilities: he must co-operate with the owner in the maintenance of the building, or that part of the building he is using, and pay a rental appropriate to the quality of the premises.
Studies of certain housing projects in Montreal have shown that tenants do not apply to their housing the share their income would justify. Thus, the 220 tenants living in the district commonly known as Victoriatown, in Montreal, were devoting an
[Mr. Loiselle.l
average of 10.8 per cent of their income to lodging while, according to the C.M.H.C. scale of rents, they should have paid twice that amount, and that without considering the cost of services. Those living in the district now occupied by "Les habitations Jeanne Mance" and the C.B.C. were in a quite identical situation.
Moreover, too often the municipal land tax, far from promoting urban redevelopment, brings about a gradual deterioration of buildings; a window made more attractive, a lawn improved, a balcony or a flight of steps repaired, are all improvements increasing the land assessment of the building and, hence, the municipal taxes.
No wonder that the owner does not repair his building which falls to pieces; consequently, the municipality's main source of income dries up instead of increasing.
The role of enterprises, institutions and public bodies must not be merely that of owners or tenants, as I outlined, but also constitute an incentive for governments and small owners, so as to promote conservation, restoration and redevelopment of properties.
If the primary responsibility for urban renewal falls on the taxpayers, the initiative must be taken by the municipality whose responsibility it is to develop a program of urban renewal.
In the field of loans for the purchase of houses, federal legislation led to significant accomplishments in the province of Quebec, but in the fields of public housing, renovation and renewal, we did not get our share.
I am not trying to blame the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. If the province of Quebec did not get its share of the amounts at the disposal of the corporation, I ascribe this to the fact that it did not have, within its administration, any commission to maintain contacts between the provincial government and municipalities and the central government. This is being settled. Unfortunately, it has taken too much time; the government of Quebec thought that other problems were more urgent. I have always said that urban renovation in the city of Montreal, just like in other areas of the province of Quebec, is a matter of urgency and must come about. I hope that the Lesage government, which will be re-elected on June 5-

May 17, 1966

is true; the member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) knows that very well but he does not want to admit it.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Two years ago last January the Montreal city council passed a motion of mine to facilitate urban renewal by private enterprise. We know that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act now provides for payment by the said corporation of up to 50 per cent of expropriation costs upon demolition of a sector. At that time, I had suggested that the city of Montreal should order some sectors torn down, after carrying out a study, with the consent of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and that, upon completion of land expropriation, this land should be resold to private concerns which would then build houses according to municipal standards and regulations, in order to give the sector a better appearance.
The fact is the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act does not now provide for the cost of renewal by private enterprise and, as a result, all fields are affected.
I have mentioned the city of Montreal, because it is my city. If it decided to expropriate certain sectors, with the agreement of the corporation, and if it could sell the land to private concerns, then the profits derived from such sales could be shared between the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the city of Montreal under a previously signed agreement. The Central Mortgage Act does not yet provide for assistance for installation of water-mains and sewage systems, for street repaving, and tree planting, etc. The act provides benefits which it is incumbent upon us to use. Unfortunately, the province of Quebec did not have in the past any opportunity to take advantage of those benefits. The city of Montreal does what it can, and in fact it adopted a building code about one year ago. By applying this code, we can prevent houses from deteriorating too fast. In some areas, we have 15- or 20-year old buildings that could be called modern slums. The building code the city council adopted will force property owners to restore and keep these buildings in good repair, so that they will not become slums which we would have to expropriate and demolish after a few years. If that building code is adequately enforced, it should accomplish a great deal.
I hope the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation will study that building code; it
Tight Money Policy
will then know what is expected. To prevent thousands of wage-earners from going into debt and tying up their future earnings in order to solve their housing problem, the federal government asked parliament to pass certain amendments to the C.M.H.C. Act during the 1964 session.
In order to remedy this situation, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act provides for credit and subsidies for the construction of low-cost dwellings. There is also an agreement between the federal and provincial governments on the construction of housing and rental units, where existing, dwellings are restored to house families in the lower income bracket.
But, as you know, when there is expropriation after agreement with the C.M.H.C., the city has to find housing for the small wage-earners. Now, the C.M.H.C. amendment of 1964 stipulated that municipalities or the provincial government could purchase certain existing buildings, renovate them and help the small wage-earners to move into them.
Renovating does not mean merely demolishing and building anew. There are two aspects to the problem: the first is the renovation of unsanitary dwellings; the other is the assistance required by families in the low income bracket.
In this regard, the Montreal city council expects to set up a three-fold system. I have already spoken of the Petite Bourgogne center that the city of Montreal is undertaking this spring and which will cover an area of 263 acres. The city of Montreal, in its eagerness to stimulate urban renewal, has found a formula which is unique in North America, I believe.
First, there is a grant for renewal. I spoke of that amendment in the last speech I made during the last parliament and I want to repeat it. This grant for renewal will help the owner who wants to repair his house according to the standards of the city of Montreal, the latter will be entitled to a certain amount according to the cost of repairs. That will help the owner who does not have the means to restore his dwelling and make it adequate.
Second, a grant for demolition and building. When we speak of housing, it is not only a matter of demolishing, as I said a while ago, for the purpose of rebuilding. In some cases, we must not raze everything to the ground. We can repair, renovate, demolish and rebuild when that must be done. In certain cases where the city would force an owner to tear down his building because it is

May 17, 1966
Tight Money Policy
not adequate or because it is substandard, the owner, if he accepts to rebuild on the same site according to the standards and regulations of the city of Montreal, will be given a grant of so many dollars by the city.
Those are advantages that, I believe, the General Housing Corporation of Quebec will make its own. I would like to see the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation include amendments concerning renovation.
Third, the city of Montreal will provide rent grants. This may seem extraordinary at first, but it is quite simple. If, by renovating, the city or a government forces a landlord to demolish and rebuild, it is logical to think that this landlord will not be able to rent the rebuilt or renovated premises for the same price as the old ones which rented for perhaps $30 or $40 a month. A modern, rebuilt apartment cannot be rented under the same conditions. That is why the city of Montreal decided to subsidize rents by giving landlords an additional amount of money fixed by the Rental Office according to the means of the head of each family, his salary, his dependents and the rent he is able to pay.
This is another amendment which would be helpful to all municipal governments wishing to make renovations. I know that all municipal administrations will not find it easy to put this amendment into practice, but I believe it can easily be done with a provincial agreement between all levels of government and the C.M.H.C.
As I said earlier, Montreal now has the "La Petite Bourgogne" project. Many other districts in the city of Montreal should be renovated, but they cannot be without the help of Quebec or the central government.
The problem of urban renewal is not confined to the metropolis. A report published some time ago showed the acuteness of the housing problem in Trois-Rivieres; a few months earlier, Quebec and, recently, West-mount found it necessary to undertake some renovation.
In considering the great cost of urban renewal, one should also bear in mind that cost is of no consequence when the health of almost half the population, the development of family life and the freedom of community life are involved.
Now, I spoke of renovation. There must certainly be other ways to remedy the situation, for it must be improved. Suggestions are not always accepted by higher authorities, but they must be made, so that the authorities may see what can be done.

Three suggestions were made in the magazine Commerce published last year. One was that the province of Quebec withdraw from the joint program offered by the national act and pass its own housing act.
It surely has deficiencies, but it also contains many provisions from which the Quebec government might take inspiration. I am not quite sure whether the Quebec government should draw up its own legislation and withdraw from this joint program. It is urgent, however, that it should take prompt action in order to help our municipalities to carry out renewal projects.
But I feel the third suggestion was the best of all. Municipalities should be left to transact business themselves with the C.M.H.C., just as other provincial governments, but part of the cost charged to municipalities should be paid, because their applications would have been approved by the C.M.H.C. This is how the "habitations Jeanne-Mance" in Montreal were built. The government of the day gave full authority to the city of Montreal to transact with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and that is how the only low-rental housing project in the province of Quebec came about. I trust that others will follow in the not too distant future, that other municipalities in the province of Quebec will be able to benefit from the Central Mortgage and Housing Act. But I would also like to see the C.M.H.C. help private enterprise, because in the field of urban renewal, it must be recognized that urban housing cannot be fully made up of low-rental dwellings; modern houses must also be built for citizens who can afford them. But private enterprise and our municipal governments must be allowed to submit such plans to the citizens of Canada. I trust that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, in addition to what it is already giving, will be able in the near future to make amendments so as to promote renewal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it a great privilege to take part in a debate of this nature on a most interesting and important subject. Because of the very word "money" and its implications and the fact that it contributes to the well-being of so many people, I feel this is a most fascinating subject. It seems to me that at this time a
May 17, 1966

repetition and careful analysis of the amendment itself might be useful. The amendment states:
The policies of the government in imposing tight money and denying builders and prospective homeowners needed mortgage funds, constitute a negative approach to the problems facing our economy and are seriously impeding the development of the nation.
That is a serious indictment, and the fact that no one speaking from the government side has attempted to explain or deny that tight money exists or has explained the reseasons for its existence is indicative of the government's failure. It is not my intention to stress the problems of housing. It is rather my intention to emphasize the general desirability of not applying uniform methods to combat the present existing situation. Uniform methods cannot be successfully applied throughout the length and breadth of this country because there is too much diversity of income, diversity of climate, diversity of general economic activity and diversity in many other ways. It is impossible for any government to adopt a uniform policy to deal with a situation which we all agree exists in this country and in the United States. I refer, of course, to the danger of inflation.
The hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) deserves credit for bringing this matter to the attention of the members of this house by way of his amendment. The events leading up to the present situation should be carefully examined with a view to understanding the actions of the government in dealing with the whole question of inflation or the danger of inflation.
In my view the government has permitted inflationary pressures to build up. Last year the money supply available in this country increased very rapidly. The government is now attempting to correct that situation but it is late in doing so. I am not one of those who suggest it is too late; I just say it is late. It has been the attitude of many speakers supporting the government that the attention of the house and the country generally should be directed to the fact that we have been enjoying a boom period. Certainly that is a correct statement, and it is a source of great satisfaction to each and every one of us that we are still enjoying a boom period.
It seems to me that the existence of a boom should bring about a need for the government to take appropriate action, but that is exactly what this government has not done. This government should have succeeded in balancing the budget during this boom period.
Tight Money Policy

maintopic: FINANCE-TIGHT MONEY POLICY-NEGATIVE APPROACH TO PROBLEMS
speechtext:
I should like to say that I am actually talking about the situation in 1964 and 1965. The minister was busy with one of his colleagues at the outset of my remarks and perhaps did not hear me say that I intended to deal with events leading up to the present situation.
I am sure hon. members would agree that it is necessary at times to indulge in deficit financing, and I would be the first person to acknowledge the truth of that under certain circumstances. I do not believe that is the case in times of booming economies. In this year of our Lord, 1966, we are faced with a situation which demands drastic action. I do not suggest it is too late to take action at this time and I am not one who is particularly pessimistic about the outcome, but the government must recognize certain basic fundamentals if it is going to deal with the situation. One fundamental that must be recognized by the government is that it cannot deal with every section of this country in the same way.
Last year we experienced a reduction in income tax and an enlargement and extension of the supply of money. However, production did not grow to the same extent as the gross national product. We should have learned from this fact that it is necessary to maintain productivity at about or more than the same level as the gross national product. Surely that is a reasonable statement. But that was not the case last year.
How does one maintain this level? That is a very good question, Mr. Speaker, and I propose to answer it to the extent I am able. I have referred to boom times and the question of deficit financing. In booming times we should balance the budget and indulge in that kind of cyclical financing which brings about a surplus in good times to provide for the proverbial rainy day. It is my observation that this sort of doctrine is not popular in this day and age. Everyone wants men and

May 17, 1966
Tight Money Policy
women in public life to get up and advocate more and more spending. In my opinion the government should have followed a different course in attempting to balance the budget.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
We heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) say in the house a few days ago that there was to be a great upsurge in capital investment this year. This we were glad to hear. But we find there has been no great curtailment in public spending. The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Keays) mentioned this in the course of his remarks. It seems to me to be a matter of ordinary common sense that in a period when private enterprise is willing to increase its investment by the almost astronomical figure of 13 or 14 per cent over last year the government should of necessity curtail some of its expenditures, particularly along certain lines. What are those certain lines? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in the important matter of credit certain steps must be taken. I happen to be one of those who went through the depression of the 1930's and I submit that looking back on those days one realizes that certain situations could have been pretty well cured had a supply of credit been available to business.
Therefore I submit that a sufficient supply of credit is one important way to meet difficult situations. In this day and age when inflation is at least considered I believe credit should be available for certain things. One is the expansion of business. My hon. friend from Northumberland in the course of his remarks said that business should be encouraged to expand. I do not think that every business should be encouraged to expand in times like these when the government-and I give them full marks in this respect-is attempting to deal with a difficult situation. Since I do not believe that every business should expand I think it is proper for me to name those that I think should expand. In this category I place first those businesses which are producing goods for export, because we have a balance of payments problem. I think we should also encourage those industries producing goods which we are importing at the present time. In my opinion these two things go pretty well together.
I think there should also be some selectivity of regions. We in the Atlantic provinces happen to be in one region of Canada where incomes are below the national average. I do not overemphasize this but it is the situation in our part of the country and it is one that

Canada as a whole has to deal with. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I submit for the consideration of the government, and especially for the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) who is in his seat, that some way should be decided upon whereby the government, faced with the special situation which exists in the Atlantic provinces, will not deal with this situation in the same way as it deals with a region of Canada where there is tremendous overactivity.
I cannot give the house any great words of wisdom in this connection, but I would refer to the so-called castor oil treatment, as it was called, and for the information of the minister I would say that I knew something about the castor oil treatment statement. In 1956 I was in a position of some public responsibility and it came to my attention that people in New Brunswick with raw materials at their disposal, with plant and personnel available and with markets for their finished products, were unable to go ahead because of the tight money policy of the then Liberal government. I was informed that the amount of money in circulation had been reduced substantially by the action of the Bank of Canada. I was told that the reason for this was inflation in the central provinces of Canada. I said, "Perhaps there is inflation in the central provinces of Canada but there is no inflation down here in the Atlantic provinces, so this sort of thing will not do."
At that time I said it would be just as ridiculous to have a uniform policy of credit availability for all ten provinces of Canada regardless of general economic conditions as it would be for a mother of ten children to give them all castor oil regardless of their individual needs. I believe the same principle applies today. Therefore I ask the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, to take this message to his colleagues in an attempt to exert moral suasion over them in order that a special program may be made available for the people of the Atlantic provinces, one of which is the minister's native province.
In this respect we find history repeating itself. Ten years later we have another Liberal government applying the same treatment to a simiar situation. So I say there should be a more liberal-with a small "1"-policy applied to the Atlantic provinces than is applied to the provinces of central and western Canada. In this connection I should like to read from the last Newsletter issued by the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council in which they speak about the question of a
May 17, 1966

special situation. It seems to me this bears repeating and placing on Hansard. The article was published in March, 1966, and says:
The general conclusion appears to be that in the Atlantic provinces, where the problem is greatest, the program has been less successful than in the rest of Canada during its initial period.
They are talking about the designated area program, but their words apply in general terms to the whole economic situation. The article goes on to say:
It is designed to meet the general Canadian problem of low income and high unemployment in small areas in an environment of high income and employment. Since the problem in the Atlantic provinces is quite different, there would appear to be no reason to anticipate that this situation will change significantly.
Then they go on to say:
In a country as large and diverse as Canada it is quite unrealistic to adhere to a rigid formula devised on broad national considerations which fail to recognize regional differences. The concern should not be with the application of a formula but with the social and economic development of a nation. There should be no great obstacles to the introduction of sufficient flexibility to permit the designation of the whole Atlantic region in the interest of its development and of Canada's.
I am not particularly arguing the latter point at the moment; I am making the point that there is this difference and I believe it should be treated as a situation different from that which exists in other parts of Canada to which these remedial measures, in so far as the danger of inflation is concerned, are being applied. I should also like to read from this document marked Exhibit B what was said at the first conference of the Atlantic provinces:
Through its monetary and fiscal policies the federal government has wide powers to control the level of economic activity in the cquntry as a whole. In the last decade, however, there have been many occasions when policies which were sound for the national economy were not suitable for the economic situation in this region. For example, a policy of high interest rates may be called for to check inflation when the economy, considered as a whole, is fully employed. But the effect of high interest rates on the Atlantic region, when resources are not fully employed, may be most adverse.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
That is the message I should like to give through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Minister of Labour, and I am sure he will give it every consideration. I return to the question of selectivity of industry. Under this heading I ask the same question which I asked before and have already answered, namely, what type of industry should be encouraged? The answer is industry which exports and industry which provides goods we now import. We
Tight Money Policy
should also pay some attention to the development of natural resources, something in which we in Canada have a natural advantage.
I am connected with a business which exports practically its whole production and always has. I also know similar types of businesses which do this. There are many other businesses of like nature which could expand but they cannot do so without credit. So again this is my basic reason for bringing to the attention of the house the fact that it is not only difficult but is not a good thing to have a fixed, rigid principle in these matters.
I am one who believes in long term loans, and by "long term" I mean 10, 12 or 15 years. There are many businesses which could expand and purchase more machinery. We must acknowledge the fact that today we are living in an age of automation. Machinery is expensive and cannot always be manufactured in Canada. Even the tooling expense is very great. If only ten machines of a certain type are made and a great tooling expense is involved, the cost becomes prohibitive. So these machines sometimes have to be brought in from the United States or some other country.
The point I am making is that to increase productivity we should buy more machinery. If people are able to borrow money over a 10, 12 or 15 year period and make repayments which are constant so they know exactly the cost per month of that machinery and equipment, then it seems to me that this is a policy which should be encouraged by the government or by any government with responsibilities to its people.
It has been said that it is incredible that industry should slow down at a time of good demand for our products in world markets. Would anyone disagree with that proposition? That is what the hon. member for Northumberland said yesterday and I am sure no one would disagree. It is incredible that industry should slow down.
The hon. member also said that sales are being lost because our prices are not competitive. I do not propose to embark upon a dissertation on the question why our products are not competitive. In many respects I think they are competitive. I think our exports are deserving, and I am sure that the minister, with his great experience in business, realizes that generally speaking we are quite competitive. So far as our steelworkers are concerned, I think they are second to none.

May 17. 1966
Tight Money Policy
I think that very often production or productivity and expansion of industry are curtailed-this is particularly so at the present time-due to the fact that people are unable to get credit and spread their repayments over a period of time. Do not the figures showing the reduction in exports prove my point? If I go back to 1965, our exports increased by a very small percentage, certainly not nearly as much as they should have increased had other methods been adopted.
It has been said that the present existing, strong inflationary pressure is caused by a shortage of goods. This brings me to the question of how we deal with inflation. Do we apply a negative policy of restricting credit or a positive policy of producing more goods? I think these are the questions which the government must answer, and they have chosen to answer them in the negative. The government have chosen to say that it is better to curtail credit. By the policy they are apparently supporting they have chosen to say it is better to reduce the amount of money available for goods than to make money available for production of more goods. That is where the matter stands at the present time, Mr. Speaker.
It has been said that we need financial incentive to increase productivity. I am one of those who believe in this doctrine. I believe that financial incentive to increase productivity is one of the ways in which industry in general and the people connected with industry can stimulate production. This goes right down to the worker himself. People with financial incentive and a production bonus are those whose business today is going full blast; they are the people working overtime. This involves reward for effort made and interest taken, and I submit that the government have the means available to do something along this line.
It has been said that the gross national product was nearly double the increase in exports last year. It has also been said that mortgage money should be provided for the average home, not for the expensive luxury home, not for the apartment house, but for the average home. I am sure we all recognize that what really builds a country are the citizens of the country who own their own homes. These citizens immediately acquire an interest in their homes and they have a stake in their country. They take great pride and care in their homes because they are theirs.

I have no reason to believe that our homebuilding policy will change. However, I submit to the minister for his consideration that if the choice lies between a big office building or apartment house and 25 or 30 small houses he should decide in favour of the small houses.
Another factor to bear in mind is that homes are very important to the expansion of industry. Expansion of industry calls for increased personnel possessed of technical knowledge and skills. The first thing these people look for in a given locality are homes to live in. I know certain areas where such homes are not available. These people require housing and schools for their children and if they are not available they will decide to go elsewhere.
It has been said-the hon. member for Northumberland made this point too-that insurance companies should invest in small towns in rural areas. I believe that is true, but the experience we have had in trying to persuade large companies to invest in this way has not been encouraging. I submit that especially in the Atlantic provinces such investment should be made.
It has also been said that the government should earmark funds for the particular purpose of providing loans. In this connection I am certain that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) would tell us that the Industrial Development Bank is available for this purpose. The Industrial Development Bank is available for the purpose, but unfortunately I do not think the Industrial Development Bank is carrying out the function for which it was established. The function for which it was established was to make term loans and provide loans Ordinary banks were not able to furnish under their charters. I believe that is the reason for having the Industrial Development Bank. However, today we find that the Industrial Development Bank is not easy to deal with. In fact, it has become a money making machine. Let me say that I am one who believes in profits. Profits make a business go. Profits make good times not bad times. I believe, however, that the Industrial Development Bank should be a little more lenient in its approach than are the chartered banks because it is allowed to be more lenient by the terms of reference that set it up.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I think it might be interesting if I were to read what has been said about the Industrial Development Bank and what it should be
May 17, 19G6

doing. I will do so, Mr. Speaker. I read from the Newsletter of March, 1966:
The bank, when considering an application for a loan, must be satisfied that the proposed project Is reasonable and sound, the management efficient, and the plan capable of carrying the additional financial burden.
No one will quarrel with that. I continue:
The money obtained through the bank may be used to purchase land and buildings, alter or enlarge existing buildings, construct new buildings, or to purchase machinery and equipment.
I think that is true. Unfortunately, it does not work out in practice. I am wondering how much the present tight money policy has to do with the attitude of the people who are administering the affairs of the Industrial Development Bank. The deputy minister of trade and commerce is, I believe a member of the board. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce were here I would ask him to carry a message to his deputy who is a director. Instead, I ask the Minister of Labour to carry my message to the director. It is: Is it not possible to be more lenient especially toward the Atlantic provinces which need the financing?
I continue reading:
The Bank does not provide funds to finance inventories or receivables, but it may in a few carefully considered circumstances-
That does not make any difference because it is a function of the chartered banks, as the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) knows.
-extend a loan to assist working capital requirements. In instances where a business may benefit from a change of ownership, the bank may consider a loan to help finance this necessary transfer.
We hear a lot of talk about United States ownership of our businesses. I am not scared of that. If somebody comes along, invests his money in Canada and is willing to comply with our laws, then he has made a contribution to the general well-being of this country. I am not a bit alarmed about that sort of thing. As a matter of fact, I know of many businesses which would not be in existence today had it not been for the financing they were able to secure in the United States.
I do not for a moment go along with those gentlemen who express fear because some people outside this country have a stake in businesses inside this country. Such people are subject to Canadian laws just as citizens of this country are. Where could we get the money to develop the country, because we have an undeveloped country, if it were not from the United States of America? I have
Tight Money Policy
seen figures as to the amount which would be required to purchase the interest now held by people in the United States. They are astronomical and so large that I could hardly quote them. It is beyond our ability to have that much money.
I now return to my subject, from which I digressed. The Newsletter continues:
Although the purposes for which the Bank may allow funds are numerous, primarily IDB is interested in the groundwork financing of a "soundly conceived new business".
I submit that a soundly conceived new business is not very much different from the expansion of an existing business. Both are going to employ more Canadians. Both are going to export and assist in helping with the general balance of payments problem.
In connection with loans I would submit that the Atlantic provinces are fertile ground for loans. As I understand it, 35 applications for loans connected with projects in the Atlantic provinces have been received, compared with 68 from the rest of Canada. On page 2 of the Newsletter there is the following:
This means that there has been about one application to every 12,600 members of the labour force in designated areas in the Atlantic provinces and one to every 8,500 in designated areas in the rest of Canada. These applications represent an investment of $35 million in the Atlantic provinces and of $101.25 million in the rest of Canada.
It should be the reverse. I do not wish to weary the house by reiterating all those things I have tried to point out to the best of my ability. I only want to summarize briefly what I have tried to say. I think the government is making a grave mistake if it tries to have a fixed and uniform credit policy applying to all parts of our great country. Conditions across the country from place to place are so very different that this would be an impractical policy.
I return now to the question before the house, our regret that the government has imposed a tight money policy. I should be interested in hearing the minister's explanation for the imposition of tight money. I should also be interested in knowing what he wishes to do with respect to mortgage funds for home owners.
I have been quite disappointed in some of the speeches which have been made in the last two days. But I repeat that this is one debate at least for which we should not apologize. Nothing could be more important than the discussion of the availability of money in Canada at the present time. Getting

May 17, 1966
Tight Money Policy
the views of all hon. members on this question is of vital importance to the nation and of interest to the government.
Therefore I say to the government that it will not be successful by having a uniformly inflexible fiscal policy for this country. I feel it should introduce some degree of flexibility with respect to credit, and when I say that I have the Atlantic provinces in mind. I also believe that businesses in general should not all be treated in the same way, that there should be diversity of enterprise, that perhaps one business ought to be encouraged at the moment and another perhaps not encouraged to the same extent.
This is the sort of message I have tried to get across. These are the sorts of things which I think deserve the consideration of the government. I appeal to the government to take some notice of the representations which have been made.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
