speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us a very serious amendment concerning the credit restrictions imposed on home builders and home buyers.
During the 1965 election campaign, I warned the people in Quebec and Canadians in general, against the credit restrictions that the government would impose on us once the campaign was over.
Since November 8, 1965, we have seen credit restrictions being imposed in the United States, urging American investors to stop or decrease their investments. In the past few months, the Minister of Finance has been telling us that the various branches of his department have to submit to credit restrictions for a certain time in many fields, and more especially in the home building field.
There is a strong tendency to slow down home building through measures as drastic and extravagant as those advocated by the government at present.
Between 1964 and 1965, there was a marked improvement in the construction field. However, this improvement has failed to meet the constant demand for housing units in our country.
Even though the demand was greater than the financial situation allowed at the time, now in 1966, a slowdown is called for in the construction field.
Mr. Speaker, I entirely disagree with the member for St. Ann (Mr. Loiselle) who said

that the C.M.H.C. has not imposed any credit restriction nor reduced the opportunities for building.
Now I think I am appealing to people who know a little more than the hon. member for St. Ann about housing construction in Canada, especially in the Ottawa-Hull area.
I have here a copy of a letter sent on April 26, 1966, to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and to the leaders of the various political parties in the house by Mr. John Hilson, president of the Building and Construction Trades Council of Hull-Ottawa and District. Here is what Mr. Hilson wrote to the Prime Minister of Canada on behalf of local builders:

Dear Sir:
Faced with the most serious unemployment in the construction trades that Ottawa has experienced for many years, I am appealing to you on behalf of the Ottawa Building Trades Council to take whatever steps are possible to substitute a program of planning for employment in place of the present situation in which we are facing planned unemployment.
At the end of March we appealed to the government to reverse its cut-back on its construction program for the Ottawa area. At that time the government had announced a cut-back of one-third of its estimates for construction in the current year for this area. The cut-back for the Ottawa area was one and a half times the total cut-back for the rest of Ontario.
We were greatly concerned at that time by the fact that of a work force of approximately 8,000 persons in the construction industry in the Ottawa area, some 1,700 were out of work representing an unemployment rate of over 20 per cent. With regard to the prospect of a seasonal improvement, we were very much discouraged by the fact that building permits issued had dropped from $25,000,000 for the first quarter of last year to $10,500,000 for the first quarter of this year.
A letter from Hon. G. J. Mcllraith made light of our concern and predicted a "general pick-up in the spring". Instead of a pick-up there has been a steady worsening in the employment situation as projects have been completed and no new projects are available to provide further employment for the workers laid off.
The Hon. G. J. Mcllraith referred to the excellent employment situation that existed during the past winter and it would appear that his optimism is based on past events rather than assessment of what is happening now and what can be expected in the future.
One of our affiliated unions which handles 90 per cent of the total structural steel erection for this area reports over 30 per cent of its members are unable to obtain employment in the Ottawa area. If the steel is not going up now, there will be further worsening of the employment opportunities for other trades in the immediate future. Other construction unions report high and worsening unemployment. Figures on unemployment among our affiliates run as high as 40 per cent, with workers leaving the area because of the poor prospeets.
May 17, 1966

The letter continues:
Since we made our previous protest, the predicted spring pick-up has failed to materialize and the construction industry is faced with further difficulties as a result of tight money. While we do have occasional conflicts of interest with our employers in the construction industry, we naturally share with them concern as to the future of our industry in this area. We sympathize with them in the difficulties and bankruptcies which are inevitable unless some positive action is taken.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that those people have the experience necessary to call the government's attention to the harmful effects which result from the application of a restrictive monetary policy.
I am wondering at this stage how it is that a government such as ours, a Minister of Finance such as ours, can find the financial means needed to make interest-free loans to foreign countries and, at the same time, with the utmost seriousness, impose credit restrictions on our own people, on those who are ready and willing to develop our country and their respective provinces.
In addition to that letter from The Building and Construction Trades Council, I have here a letter from the provincial Association of Building Contractors of Quebec, from the town of Mount Royal, to the effect that the president of that association supports the Henry report on housing.
Mr. Fernand Boisse, of Sherbrooke, president of that association says:
The report prepared by Mr. Robert Henry, editor in chief of Bdtiment, for the Association of Building Contractors of Montreal, Includes all the problems which the housing industry must face in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, the president of that association of building contractors must certainly know as much about that matter as the hon. member for St. Ann who tells us that there is no restriction.
We know that in all our ridings the C.M.H.C. is subject to restrictions ordered by the government, which hamper the building of houses.
Are they trying to prevent the construction of houses because people are well accommodated in our cities or urban areas? Are they not rather preventing the construction of such houses because there is a shortage of funds, in other words, a shortage of credit?
And when there is a shortage of credit, Mr. Speaker, one never hears a minister blame that monetary policy.
Tight Money Policy
I heard the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) former premier of New Brunswick, tell us: If we cannot borrow from the United States, what will we do? The United States are there to supply us with the funds needed to keep up our construction or development.
Mr. Speaker, the ministers, the government, even each federal member should consider this very important question: How is it that the United States are able to loan money to every country in the world and, at the same time, not borrow from any of them? No one is asking himself that question. Where is the money that the United States can supply to the whole world coming from? Loans to Viet Nam, loans to Russia, loans to Canada, loans to any country in the world. And the United States never borrow a nickel or penny from any country whatsoever. Who is making the credit of the United States?
Does credit grow on trees in the United States more than in Canada?
I stress that point, Mr. Speaker. When we have here, in Canada, the necessary brains, good will, materials and physical possibilities to build houses so as to lodge our people adequately, why do we have, to ask the United States permission to build housing units or develop our natural resources?
Why do we not put our financial system in order, instead of always suggesting to the people to tighten their belt, and putting our builders on the brink of bankruptcy with tight money policies? Why do we always have to ask permission from the United States? Who makes credit in the United States? Where do they get the credit or the money they need to lend billions of dollars to Canada?
Were the United States concerned about knowing whether there was not enough money to develop Ungava, in Quebec? Were the United States short of credit to buy the oil production of Alberta and the western provinces? No indeed. The United States monetary problem is settled on the spot. Why? Because the magnates, those in control, live there, and they are the ones who give orders to countries like ours.
And people talk about parliament's supreme authority, Canada's sovereignty, Canada's independence.
In the field of housing, Mr. Speaker, do we need the United States' permission to build small houses? Do we need the United States' permission to clear away the slums in the

May 17, 1966
Tight Money Policy
city of Montreal, for instance? And we know how many slums there are, not only in the city of Montreal, but in every city. We see slums in all cities, all towns and villages, in the country all over Canada. Are we short of materials, as I said a moment ago, to replace these slums by sound houses? No. We have everything except credit. And because we do not have credit, the building of houses is restricted. That is why this tight money policy is inadmissible.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I consider well-advised the amendment moved yesterday by the opposition to the effect that the policies of the government, in imposing tight money and denying builders and prospective home owners needed mortgage funds, constitute a negative approach to the problems facing our economy and are seriously impeding the development of the nation. It is admitted that these tight money policies seriously impede the development of our country.
I go on quoting the letter of the Quebec province Association of Building Contractors.
Mr. Boisse says:
It will be recalled that during the recent construction strike in Montreal, a brief had been prepared and released to the press as well as to the highest provincial and federal authorities. The brief, entitled "Survey of the residential industry and the causes threatening its immediate disappearance" contains a full statement, based on statistics, of the causes of deterioration of an industry essential to the public: housing.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Mr. Fernand Boisse, who has long been striving to secure for the housing industry the right to negotiate labour agreements with the unions, adds: The day is past when the builders kept mum, leaving the industry at the mercy of the government's lack of interest. Everyone, the ministers first of all, must now realize once and for all that the housing industry is not an economic endeavour like the others and that vague slum clearance projects will not solve the No. 1 problem of Quebec families: to own their homes and to be adequaiely housed at reasonable prices. Slum clearance is not enough, says Mr. Boisse, but new ones must be prevented from developing. Only through direct association between private industry-that is the builders-and the General Housing Corporation can the government adequately solve problems that are not only administrative, but also technical and human problems.
The Henry Report, adds Mr. Boisse, perfectly represents the position of our industry: On the brink. It also indicates that the builders are not alone on the brink: any threat to the housing industry involves the people's right to own their homes and to be adequately housed.
Mr. Fernand Boisse adds: "We have asked again and again that a builders union be authorized under which would permit to select of builders, clean up the market, progress and serve the public
[Mr. Caouette.l
better. The provincial government has only to append its signature. But it is essential for the public. Our request is sensible:	electricians,
plumbers, real estate operators all have unions. Why is the builder, who hires such plumbers and electricians and has the responsibility for those houses and apartments, why should he not be entitled to a union?
This is obviously under provincial jurisdiction.
Home builders and the public, adds Mr. Boisse, will no longer be satisfied with promises, still less with silence.
The provincial Association of Building Contractors of Quebec comprises nine local associations covering the whole province, namely Montreal, Quebec, Sherbrooke, Hull, Bois-Francs, Saguenay, Lake St. John, Joliette, Drummondville, Thetford Mines and almost all residential housing.
Here is a testimonial to the fact that credit restrictions are unacceptable in a country where everything remains to be done, in a country where tens of thousands of homes are lacking to house our people properly. And contractors from the Ottawa area, Mineault Desnoyers Construction, write to us along the same lines:
Mr. Desnoyers says:
The home building industry in the Hull area is deeply hurt by the credit restrictions of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the lending companies.
A member of the government has just said that C.M.H.C. does not impose any restrictions. It is obvious that the housing construction industry is now in utter chaos. In his letter, Mr. Desnoyers continues:
The majority of the housing projects in the area are financed by C.M.H.C. Because of the small number of loan companies that grant direct loans in our region, the C.M.H.C. remains the main source of mortgage loans.
When the buyer of a house asks the C.M.H.C. to finance him, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) tells him to go to private enterprise, insurance companies, those that lend money outside C.M.H.C. Why then was it created? Why was it instituted? To serve the people or to annoy them?
Yesterday, my colleague for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) said, and rightly so, that the present government drains individual and company earnings into the purchase of government bonds, and the government endeavours to finance individuals and private companies. It is not up to the government to do that. Its duty is to see that the public in general is treated fairly and reasonably. C.M.H.C. was created precisely to facilitate the removal of slums in Canada and the
May 17, 1966

building of dwellings to house our Canadian families. And Mr. Desnoyers pursues:
These measures put us, the builders, in a desperate situation where huge amounts have already been committed through the purchase of land or other agreements.
This causes losses and considerable increase in the cost of operations. The housing construction market will be flooded with requests for mortgage loans and applicants will be refused the required funds. We maintain that the present restrictions are inflationary and that they beneflt profiteers who give conventional loans at usurious and prohibitive rates of interest.
To conclude, we protest energetically against that policy which we consider to be discriminatory to one particular industry which gives employment to thousands of workers.
In this case, Hull is concerned in particular, but we know the problem exists everywhere.
In my own area, I have asked time and time again the C.M.H.C. to open an office in Rouyn-Noranda. Those two cities have a total population of 35,000 inhabitants. It is an area inhabited by more than 150,000 people and the C.M.H.C. does not give us any answer. The government does not take a stand.
According to reports made on television, Abitibi would be an underdeveloped area where there are slums. There are no more than in the city of Montreal. But the problem is not solved. We need the help of the C.M.H.C. We do not want the corporation to own those houses, but we want it to help private enterprise make possible adequate and low cost housing, for our Canadian families.
And Mr. Desnoyers says in his letter:
In closing, we strongly protest against this policy we think unfair for a particular sector of industry that provides employment for thousands of workers. In view of those facts, we demand that measures be taken immediately to free the direct loan market and that private companies be forced to put up the required funds for loans guaranteed by C.M.H.C. We support any other measure that will contribute to rectify this systematic freezing of funds to the detriment of our industry and our people. Remedial action is needed immediately and any delay can only make the situation increasingly serious.
Desnoyers Construction Ltee.
And it is signed: Charles Desnoyers, President.
I cautioned the Canadian people against credit restrictions in November 1965. Now, those people did not believe in credit restrictions. As a matter of fact, the government loudly stated that credit would never be restricted. They even said then, as Jean Lesage now claims, that I was a witch-hunter. The sorcerers and the witches are in the
Tight Money Policy
government now, and it is true that we are going to hunt away as much as we can, because we cannot admit credit restrictions in a country where everything remains to be done, where everything has to be built.
We have a Canadian people that is capable, determined to develop what has to be developed in this country and credit restrictions laid down by the federal government are going to slow down the progress of business in Canada.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The government should be the first to object to that restrictive policy which is preposterous. And yet the same government is so open-handed with the funds it gives to foreigners. Was there any discussion at all on the grant of $1,625,000 to Jamaica for the construction of a sewer system, for the construction of a bridge, for the construction of a highway in the region? That 60-year loan to Jamaica was interest-free.
The government quite readily makes interest-free loans to foreigners, but it makes interest-bearing loans through C.M.H.C. to house Canadians. Then the government says it is impossible to do otherwise and that, in these times, we must tighten our belts and accept sacrifice. Have the Canadian people not made enough sacrifices in the past to serve the magnates of finance and the Canadian and American bankers who control the economic blood of the nation? Open-handedness or liberalities for foreigners; restrictions for Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to repeat that I see no objection to our assisting underdeveloped countries such as Jamaica, Tobago or Commonwealth countries located in the Caribbean. I agree that we should help them, but let us at least help our own citizens. How can we help others, if we are not able to help our own people?
All slums are not done away with. What happens now, with the restrictions on credit? We create poverty. The government gives the restrictions its blessing and, instead of fighting poverty, it now fights the poor.
It is nobody's secret that when we go through lower Montreal, we can meet people earning less than $2,400 per annum, workers who live in slums, and I would even say, in dog houses. Mr. Speaker, we allow people to live in such houses. Canadian mothers, fathers and children presently live in dreadful conditions in the very city of Montreal, the

May 17, 1966
Tight Money Policy
metropolis of Canada, the second Frenchspeaking city in the world. Slum areas still exist, not only in Montreal but in Toronto.
I was in Brockville yesterday and I saw slums there. They are everywhere, in spite of our having the means and the power to make them disappear and provide adequate housing for our people; but credit restrictions are allowed, ostensibly to fight inflation while actually the contrary is true.
Credit restrictions will raise interest rates. When interest rates rise of course houses cost more. The government runs true to form after levying the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. On the one hand, the government generously grants a $500 bonus for winter-built houses then it turns around and slaps a sales tax on building materials which raises by $1,000 the cost of a $13,000 to $14,000 house.
The government thinks it is generous to the Canadian people. Why always crush those who are building up the country? Are we here to crush the Canadian people or to serve them? We are here to serve the people; let us then serve them instead of kotowing to the big financial interests. Then perhaps we will have found an acceptable solution.
The other day, I heard the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Berger) repeat his charges whereby we, the creditistes, are always concerned with one and the same thing: money. What about the government? It is always concerned with the same thing. What is credit restriction? Instead of issuing money when the economy is buoyant, when Canadian production can reach a new high the money is restricted to punish the Canadian people. Well, the Canadian people, the population of the province of Quebec, will not put up very long with this policy of restriction.
Mr. Speaker, we have had our fill of these far-fetched solutions which always mean that finance must be protected and that the Canadian people must foot the bill. I think that the classes of Canadian society have suffered enough in the past from this belttightening policy, which allows poverty to exist in the midst of plenty.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude my remarks by saying that what Canada needs at present is a policy of credit expansion according to our possibilities. And I repeat now that the point is not at all to issue money or credit without any consideration, but to develop the country,

build houses and develop our natural resources according to our physical possibilities and our capacity.
In a few days, we will consider the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce. The minister knows the facts because he is aware of our great possibilities, not only in the province of Quebec but all over Canada.
We should consider these physical possibilities and adjust our financial system accordingly. I am convinced that we would then serve the best interests of the Canadian nation as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must confess that when I listened yesterday to the remarks of the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) which preceded his amendment I felt somewhat like the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowiehan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) in that I found great difficulty in deciding just where the hon. member was heading. His remarks were interesting, but I wondered about their direction.
Yesterday there happened to be an observer in the house-not a member I might add

who supplied the answer to my question about the hon. member's remarks. This morning he was thoughtful enough to draw my attention to an address that was prepared and delivered by the hon. member for Northumberland in Lindsay, Ontario, on May 13 to the Ontario Municipal Association. I myself address municipal organizations on occasion because I find they provide a good forum for political speeches. Rather, it was because of the fact that the hon. member's speech was a political speech delivered to a political association that I found myself in the same difficulty as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, because the unconnected political speech preceded the motion.
If you compare that speech with the speech delivered by the hon. member in the house yesterday, you will find that the last five and a half pages are much the same as the last four columns of the hon. member's remarks as they appear in Hansard for yesterday. There was one difference. The hon. member was speaking in generalities. He spoke about tight money in generalities, he spoke about immigration, high-rise apartments, luxury suites and other things in generalities, but he never did mention any facts or figures to support these general statements.
May 17, 1966

The hon. member did make some statements about immigration. In that lies the one difference. He said employment had been increasing steadily for the past five years in Canada and that we should have opened the doors to more immigrants. I agree entirely that we need more immigrants and that we should open our doors and welcome them. I am proud to say that I played some part in doing just that, opening and holding open the doors. The figures on immigration for the last nine years will reflect what I have said.
In the year 1958, the first full year in which the official opposition was in power, the total number of immigrants admitted to Canada was 124,851. In 1959 that number dropped to 106,928. In 1960 it dropped still further to 104,111. In 1961 the figure dropped to 71,689. In 1962 the figure was slightly higher but still only 74,586. In 1963, the first year in which this government took office and we were in office for only two-thirds of that year, immigration jumped from 74,000 in 1962 to 93,151 in 1963, to 112,606 in 1964 and to 146,758 in the year in which I happened to be the minister. That is more than double what it was for the last two years when the hon. member for Northumberland was a member of the former government.
I am happy to say that the indications are that as a result of the change in immigration policy which has taken place over the last two years there will be a still higher figure, with an additional 20,000 to 30,000 immigrants coming into Canada in 1966, many of them with skills and others with strong backs and aptitudes which will make them desirable citizens of this country.
I said I found it difficult to follow the remarks of the hon. member, but I also felt that his remarks on immigration should not go unchallenged. In the light of the remarks not only of the proposer of the motion but in light of the tenor of the remarks of other speakers during the course of the last day and a half, it might be appropriate and perhaps helpful at this time if I spoke briefly about some of the facets of our housing situation.
Most of the speakers have been prone to ignore and forget the real facts of this troublesome period in our housing history. It is my sincere hope that a frank expression of a few thoughts on a matter of such national economic and social significance may assist us to have a better over-all view of the picture. It is, of course, no secret that all of us in this house have been the recipients of, I would
Tight Money Policy
say, a massive aggregate number of telegrams, letters and other communications from organizations and individuals. The hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) has just read two or three of them. We have received this correspondence during recent weeks. The main purpose of all this correspondence is to ensure that the cabinet and other members of parliament are fully cognizant of the difficulties being encountered in obtaining adequate mortgage financing for the year 1966 in respect of residential construction.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
It is quite likely that this correspondence accounts largely for the motion we are now debating. But another purpose of the correspondence is undoubtedly to prod the government into finding a solution for this problem, trying to put it on the shoulders of the government. I am very sorry that the hon. member for Northumberland and the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) are not here because they have both come forward as friends of free enterprise. In fact, we heard the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton bragging about it this afternoon. There is no reason why he should apologize for being a great believer in free enterprise; I happen to be one myself. But I ask hon. members to keep in mind constantly that what has happened has been brought about by the free action of the private lending institutions in this country and is a direct result of the great prosperity, the boom in which we now find ourselves.
On this point I should like to make two or three very brief comments. I am prompted to do so by some of the remarks the hon. member for Villeneuve made just a few moments ago. He referred to letters that had been sent and had been unanswered. I should like to assure the house that I have probably received more letters on the subject of housing than any other member of the house, and there is not a single letter on housing that has come into my office up to 48 hours ago that has not been answered and answered promptly.

speechtext:
The suggestion that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the government are trying to refrain from or are afraid of answering questions is just not in accordance with the facts, and my files show it. In this connection, it might be well if I read a letter to which I sent to the president

May 17. 1966
Tight Money Policy
of the National House Builders Association, Mr. Gelinas, whose name has been mentioned more than once in the debate this afternoon. Mr. Gelinas is a friend of mine. I thanked him for his telegram of May 9 and went on to say:
In my recent statement in the House of Commons I stated that the government would continue to take every step necessary to ensure a program of direct mortgage loans by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at the same level as that of last year when, including the fall program, loans for approximately 31.500 units were approved. I would hope that this announcement will assure the builders that there will be no contraction in the corporation's direct lending program this year.
The corporation will again make loans available for the autumn and winter building period, and expects to begin accepting applications for this aspect of the program in August.
I will have something to say on the significance of that date later. My letter continues:
The assurance that funds will be available to the same extent as last year will also enable the corporation to meet the most urgent needs arising in the early summer, particularly in the resource development areas and certain other areas where the rapid expansion of industry has caused special problems.
Here again I would pause to draw this to the attention of the hon. member for Vic-toria-Carleton and others who spoke on this subject and commented on the need and importance of making provision in these special areas. The letter continues:
I know you are aware that the direct lending program of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation cannot meet all of the demands arising from a buoyant market, and builders may not be able to obtain all the direct loans they desire. Nevertheless the corporation will do everything possible to meet the most urgent housing needs with the funds available.
The government has recognized for the past several months that Canada was approaching a period of restricted mortgage financing for new house construction. Indeed, as far back as the summer of 1965 we were aware of what might happen, as was everybody else who knew the facts, including the members of the National House Builders Association. Bulletins were sent out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation drawing their attention to the situation, drawing their attention to what might normally happen in the last three months of last year and the first three or six months of this year. I would point out in this connection that while the housing figures are rather interesting there has not been the catastrophic state of affairs that some people would

have you believe and as many of the messages which have been sent to members of this house would indicate.
In 1958 we had a good year in housebuilding; 146,686 houses were completed. But by
1961	that number had dropped to 115,608. In
1962	it was slightly higher, 126,682. In 1963 it was 128,191, and in 1964 the figure had jumped to roughly 151,000 houses, a record year. The year 1965 was another record year, 153,037 houses having been completed. Hon. members were led to believe that we were going to fall woefully short of what was done last year and I immediately rose to challenge that, because a simple statement of the facts will show how false it is.
In the biggest year we ever had in housing in this country we completed 153,037 homes. That was last year. In January of this year, due to the accent that had been placed on winter home building and to the switch in financial arrangements, we had 120,000 houses actually under construction, and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation provided in the first month of this year funds for another 15,000 houses. This makes a total of 135,000 already as against 153,000 in the best year we ever had.
In addition, realizing that because of the play of economics and of supply and demand the private, traditional lenders were making funds available for the building of office buildings and for industry and that for other people interested in mortgage money these funds were not being made available, the government announced, so that housebuilders could plan intelligently, that we would make funds available for direct lending for another 16,500 houses. So you have a total of 151,500 houses in 1965 without any more money from the private lenders, and do hon. members think for one moment that with the principles enunciated in the budget there is not in the next few weeks going to be some additional private money made available for housebuilding?
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I mentioned in my remarks on the budget that firms which are building pulp and paper mills and other great industrial plants in the country realize that substantial savings will be made due to the fact that no sales tax will be payable on machinery and equipment in 1968 and that a substantial reduction will be made in 1967. I am glad the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton has returned to the house because I want to say that I agree with his
May 17, 1966

remarks that we should not in this day and age curtail investment in industries which are expanding to take care not only of our export needs but our essential needs at home, but particularly our needs in the export field. The hon. member stressed the desirability of balancing our payments with other nations. I agree with him.
I should like to point out, however, to the hon. gentleman that he, having served with distinction as Canada's first minister of forestry, will be very conscious of the fact that in 1963 a survey was made of world requirements for forest products. We know that by 1975 there will be an increased demand over 1963 of approximately 50 per cent. We also know-figures are available in the library and in the Department of Forestry to show this -that this great pent-up demand will not manifest itself at the present time but will appear in about 1973 and 1974. Therefore, why should we build industrial plants now which can be built in 1968, 1969 and 1970 in good time to take care of this demand? It is really a question of priorities. As soon as this is realized by industry and the financial people I am sure we will find there is more money available for housing and other developments in the country.
Another interesting suggestion made by the hon. member for Northumberland, whose motion we are now considering, is this. He said-and this was a most extraordinary statement coming from the lips of a man who sat on the treasury benches for several years -that attention should be given to changing the interest rate. I should like to quote his words as reported at page 5175 of yesterday's Hansard:
One of the main difficulties is that the federal government has not been able to keep insurance and trust companies interested in lending on a low interest . . . basis-
I am omitting a few words.
This was partly due to the government increasing the interest rate. When the rate rose above 6 per cent the banks, of course, were eliminated from N.H.A. financing.
A law student or any person with any knowledge of the Bank Act, Mr. Speaker, knows that banks cannot lend money on mortgages for housing purposes regardless of the interest rate. Perhaps this situation should be corrected and in time it may be, but you cannot get money from banks at 6 per cent interest simply by directing a change in the interest rate or by reducing it to 6 per cent because banks are barred entry into the field
Tight Money Policy
of first or second mortgages on real estate or anything of that nature.
It might also be well to recall that mortgage money was in plentiful supply in the first half of 1965, as it was during all of 1964. This resulted in the unusually high activity in house-building to which I have referred. In 1964 it was high; in 1965 housebuilding was up 8.3 per cent over 1964. However, after July 1, 1965, funds from traditional lenders became increasingly scarce; yet in spite of that we had a record housebuilding year. It was in this atmosphere, an atmosphere which I say had already cast its shadow in July, 1965, that the government undertook on January 7 of this year, and undertook only after very exhaustive examination, to increase the national housing maximum rate from 6J to 6| per cent.
As a direct result of this, Mr. Speaker, I am sure not ten members of the house realize that national mortgage lending by approved lenders during the first two and a half months of this year was higher than it was in the same months in 1965 and 1964. I have already indicated that we will come to within about 10 or 15 per cent of last year's record level, perhaps even closer to that level.
However, having said that I believe in the free enterprise system, and many of those who have taken part in this debate having said the same thing, I am sure we will all agree that we cannot legitimately criticize approved lenders, whether they be life insurance companies, trust companies or any other lending institution, for lending their money to sources from which they get the best rate of return. That is only normal business and it is something which is governed by the law of supply and demand.
It is now apparent that the increase in long-term bond interest rates has offset the stimulus given loans for housing purposes in the first two and a half months of this year. I am sure that when the effect of the budget becomes apparent the pendulum will begin to swing in the opposite direction. I am not sufficient of a prophet, nor have I a crystal ball, to say how far the swing will go but it seems inevitable that a swing will begin in this direction.
While I have said more than once that the federal government would make available for direct lending no less amount of money that it made available last year to ensure the construction of another 31,500 units during the calendar year 1966, or possibly I should say housing starts during the latter part of

May 17, 1966
Tight Money Policy
the year, I think we must recognize that for an indefinite period the conventional lenders are going to make an election which it is open to them to make in a country such as ours, namely, whether to invest in office buildings, apartment blocks, private homes or in industry, as they see fit.
I think that the reason for the decreased participation in lending for housing purposes on the part of conventional lenders during the last two or three months is understandable to anyone who really believes in the free enterprise system. Particularly in a burgeoning economy we cannot always spread our bread with butter on both sides. In other words, we must always consider priorities. Where one demand is more urgent than another, that is the one to which we are most likely to respond.
What I say now may not apply to all of my hon. friends in the house. We are not all businessmen. Some of them have different political beliefs and ideologies from mine, and, of course, I respect them. But those of us who have had a business background, and I think that all reasonably well informed members of the house, should not lose sight of the fact that when financial institutions lend money it is their job, as the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton pointed out, to make a reasonable profit for themselves. If these institutions can get an extra half of 1 per cent or three quarters of 1 per cent out of one sound investment as against another, then that is their privilege; and when that happens no one should criticize.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
When you have houses being built within a small margin of the number built during the record year you can hardly expect the government, if it believes in the free enterprise system, to bail out housebuilders or anyone else at a time when for the first time in 13 years they are beginning to feel a little pressure during the spring and summer months of the year. Instead of coming to the government for help I suggest that they do a little soul searching or a little fiend searching, that they go to the financial institutions in their own ridings, of which there are many in this country, including insurance companies, mortgage companies and others and try their luck there.
Instead of directing their appeals to the 264 hon. members of this house, why should not the builders, the National Housebuilders Association, the chambers of commerce, the

labour organizations and the agricultural and other organizations direct them to the private lending institutions, pointing out to them that it is good business not to switch completely from one line of investment at this particular time but to put money into mortgages. A little effort like that, I am inclined to think, would bring about results.
The government, in its policy announced regarding the provision of direct lending in the same amount as last year, is dealing with a situation that cannot be ignored. As has been stated more than once by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and by others, the keynote of the budget is moderation. We want to extend, to spread out our prosperity.
Reference was made by the hon. member for Villeneuve to shortages of houses in the Ottawa-Hull area. I respectfully submit to each and every hon. member that you can see some vacant houses and vacant apartments in this area every day of the week. In fact, Ottawa is overbuilt as regards houses. There is greater need for housing in communities such as Prince George, Gold River and Vancouver island than here. There is a greater need for houses around the borders of the city of London and in southwestern Ontario where the automotive complex is situated, than in some of the larger urban areas of this country. All the government is saying is: "Let us spread it out".
There is no doubt that when the billion dollar expansion programs we are now engaged in are completed there will be plenty of housing. However, there may be some inconvenience to some people during the next year or so.
I would ask hon. members to bear in mind what has happened in other countries which have become industrialized. We have become more heavily industrialized in Canada in the last 23 years than in the preceding 100 years. When one looks at countries such as Sweden, Germany, France and Russia, which have been putting emphasis on and stressing the importance of new production facilities of the kind that the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton mentioned today, it will be seen that they all emphasize completing the plants that are going to create jobs and then building houses as quickly as possible thereafter. That is what we are trying to do at this time.
I think our housing policy today reflects that thinking. In the budget, Mr. Speaker, there was no element of panic, no lack of confidence, no suggestion of a diminishing faith in this country. Our examination of the
May 17, 1966

facts has led us to quite a different conclusion which is that we are in every way sound and strong and a great nation. However, there is a limited amount of skilled labour available; there are limited amounts of certain building materials; there is a limited amount of money in the hands of private lenders.
May I just quote some figures. When we built a record number of 153,000-odd houses last year in this country, how many do hon. members think were actually financed by the government? The figure is 31,500 with direct loans, similar to this year's announced figure, and roughly another 24,000 by way of guaranteed loans. But 100,000 houses in Canada were built with moneys provided without government money or guarantees of any kind, with moneys provided by the conventional lenders of this country.
Is anyone sufficiently childish to suggest, because for the first time there is pressure during the spring and summer months of the year to build more houses at once, that the government should step in? The builders quite naturally would like to keep building at the same level they have achieved during the last three years. They would like to continue doing that each year. To enable them to do that the private lending institutions would have to lend, as they did last year, $1,5G0 million.Were the government to step into the field, in addition to the approximately $450 million it has made available, it would have to provide another $1,500 million. Frankly, that would not make sense to me. Nor would that sort of thing make sense in the other countries to which I have referred which are placing primary importance on the need for industrialization, particularly where they have raw materials that can be converted to secondary and tertiary products, and placing lesser importance on other things.
I would not want anyone to create the slightest impression that housing is not considered by the government to be of the utmost importance. It has a high level of priority. It is because it has such a high level of priority that the government has taken the actions it has. I submit that in recent years we have clearly demonstrated our attitude. One only needs to look at the record of the last three years or so to see that.
In addition to the types of housing I have referred to, the 150,000-odd houses that were built last year and the 140,000 or possibly the
150,000	that we expect will be built this
Tight Money Policy
year, other types of housing are very important. In these fields there has been and is no curtailment. Instead, there has been every encouragement by the government.
Only this afternoon while sitting in the house I signed submissions that should bring into being hundreds of units of public housing in the province of Ontario alone. In 1965,
4,000	housing units were authorized compared with only 600 in 1964. It is true that most of this activity was in the province of Ontario, and I must give them credit for doing so much. What was done was done with public money, 90 per cent of which was supplied by the federal government through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I also want to make it perfectly clear that in addition to the funds for the direct financing of 31,500 loans and in addition to the guarantees there will be no diminution in funds for public housing. As a result we not only have public housing being built in Ontario on this very encouraging scale but also in other parts of Canada. Apart from the greatly expanded volume of public housing, an extensive program of low-rental housing for the elderly and for families with restricted incomes is now also being carried out -there is no restriction in that field-with N.H.A. assistance to private and publicly sponsored limited-dividend and non-profit corporations. Loans of this type amounted to more than $14 million in 1965, with a substantially higher amount being indicated for 1966. These projects will increase the number of housing units that will be made available to people with low incomes, to senior citizens and to others in this country.
We cannot have everything at once, Mr. Speaker. At this point in our national development it is not likely that we can have everything at once. The important thing in the field of housing is to do the right thing so that we take care of what one might term the important or urgent needs.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Admittedly in the field of housing there still exists a buoyant demand. We would not want it otherwise. We shall have an opportunity to take care of any demand that we have not supplied this year during next year or the year after next. Having said this, however, I would be derelict if I were to suggest there were no immediate or serious housing problems in Canada. I see in the house today members from constituencies to

May 17. 1966
Tight Money Policy
which these remarks apply. I refer for instance to housing in southwestern Ontario, to places in Labrador and Quebec, to parts of Manitoba, Alberta, Saskatchewan and many sections of British Columbia following the huge industrial development there.
There are other needs in the housing field, for example, housing for Indians. Only a few weeks ago my colleague the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) announced a housing program of vital significance to every decent-minded person in this country. I happen to know something about it because I participated in some of this work. I visited 20 of the Indian communities last summer. I saw the housing conditions in which they live. I noted the absence of electrification, which is an almost indispensable part of housing today. The northerly parts of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia are regions where normally the days are short and the nights are long. An Indian child may get home from school at 4.30. How can he read a book if his home is not properly lit?
This is a type of housing that I happen to consider as being of great importance, more important in my opinion than some of the high-rise luxury apartments referred to by the hon. member who moved the motion we are considering. The government is not ignoring this need; in fact, $112 million is being put into this kind of housing and improvements.
All things taken into consideration, the government has no apologies to make about the adequacy of the moneys it is making available for housing. If time permitted I should like to deal with some of the points which have been raised by hon. members, but I believe the time allotted to me has almost expired. I agree with the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton that no uniform inflexible money policy is advisable. I hope hon. members will have gathered from what I have already said that we are not following an inflexible policy. Even in our present program priorities are being adhered to and applied in the case of low income citizens, Indians and others with special needs.
Perhaps I might conclude this statement by reiterating an observation I made in this house on April 27 when I referred to the housing situation and said:
The situation is serious, but I am happy to say, as a result of studies I personally have made in conjunction with senior officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, that while it is more

serious in a few areas than in most others, it is not as serious as one would be led to believe by the telegrams and messages coming to members of this house.
I trust hon. members will agree with that comment after the short analysis I have been able to give this afternoon. We are being subjected to pressure by people who have certain interests. They are not to be blamed for trying to foster their interests. But we must be strong enough to resist this pressure and go along in accordance with priorities which we believe are in the best interests of this country.
The government and its advisers keep a close watch on the housing situation and other factors where credit is involved, and because of this and because of the facts I have stated in the house this afternoon I urge all members to vote against the motion put forward by the hon. member for Northumberland.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to say that I think the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) might well have caught your eye first, and I want to place on record the courtesy he has extended me in allowing me to make my few remarks. No doubt, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) is occupied with other duties, but I want to put on record the situation in my own constituency regarding housing. The last report available for the month of April indicates that single unit housing starts in Regina totalled 47 as compared with 104 last year. The situation in regard to mortgage money is such that although a local survey indicated an absolute minimum need of 1,200 housing units this year, it is not expected that more than 800 will actually be constructed.
This is a critical situation and I want to place it before the minister. I do not think he intended to indicate in his remarks that the people who have made representations to hon. members of this house have made false representations. Perhaps they have overemphasized part of the situation, but I think the figures I have quoted indicate that there is a serious situation in the industry.
I am one who believes that government intervention in the private sector should be limited when the private sector is able to look after itself, but when pressures on the private sector are such that there are needs it cannot fill, then I believe government intervention is warranted.
Although there was a high level in housing construction last year, in fact a record level as the minister said, the pressures for more housing in certain categories, over and above subsidized housing and housing for the aged, are greater now than they were last year. Therefore a cutback in the program at this time does not lend itself to achieving the aims of what government policy should be.

May 17, 1965
Tight Money Policy
It is to be regretted that the government has taken the position it has at this time. The situation I have pointed out in Regina is similar to the pressures and needs found in the northern area, in the city of Saskatoon and its adjacent areas. Industrial development, particularly potash mining, in that area is creating a greater need for housing units.
The suggestion that contractors should turn to other lenders for funds is rather facetious because we know funds have dried up. At the present time there are just not sufficient funds available, and what funds are available are being lent at such high interest rates that they do not provide the moderate type of housing that is required, for instance, houses in the $13,000 to $16,000 category. One of the mistakes the government made in its policy was to raise to $18,000 the maximum value of a house under N.H.A. legislation. The minister suggests that sufficient money will be provided to equal the 31,000 housing starts made last year, but I suggest that more money will be needed. Because of the higher price of houses the government's policy will be affected.
We have a so-called war on poverty, but the results of the government's policy will be to put pressure on people who are outside the range of that war. I do not think this is good. I do not want to take up a lot of time, Mr. Speaker, since there are only a few minutes left before the taking of the vote. 1 have put the situation in Regina on record. The minister has had representations on it. I know the people concerned feel the situation is so critical that they are going to make representations to the minister through other sources, and these representations will reach him in a different manner. I am quite willing to let him judge what they are, as I am not going to tell him now.
Another matter I want to bring to hon. members' attention has to do with the fairness of governmental decisions, and in this I am not critical of the minister because I do not think the final decision has yet been made. I have no quarrel with the extension made in connection with homes in flooded areas of Manitoba, where work had to stop due to floods. But the fact that a strike took place in Regina and continued beyond the deadline that houses had to be completed was just as devastating as the floods. In Regina at present there are some 25 units that are affected, and unless the government decides that the strike was responsible, payment in

respect of these houses will not be made. I believe the government should extend the period for completion of the houses, now that the strike is over. That is only reasonable and fair.
There was absolutely nothing that could be done to complete these homes while the strike was in progress. We all recognize that labour has a right to strike in order to satisfy its own demands, and in a case like this the government should give recognition to the situation. I believe representations have been made to the government about these houses and I ask the minister to give sympathetic consideration to those representations so that the situation may be corrected.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very glad to yield the floor to the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More), and I sort of wished he would talk the clock out because in five minutes there is very little comprehensive analysis that one can make of the minister's speech. However, that will keep until his estimates are before the house, at which time we can go into it more fully.
If there is anything evident from the minister's speech this afternoon, it is what we have been saying for many months in this bouse, namely that there is no housing policy here in Ottawa, no national, comprehensive housing policy at all. It is sort of like a yo-yo policy: It goes up and down. It is like a tap one turns on: When he wants to increase employment and help expansion, he throws a lot of mortgage money on the market and hopes something good will come of it.
The minister took a lot of time this afternoon to heap mountains of self-congratulatory praise upon himself, and pointed out what a wonderful job the government was doing because it was going to fall only 15 per cent below the housing target. I suggest that some time between now and the time when his estimates come before the house, the minister take a pretty serious look at the National Housing Act because N.H.A. should more accurately be called the national hoaxing act.
When it was brought into effect, I believe in 1945, it was a genuine workingman's act. Houses were selling for $6,000 at that time. Mortgages were issued for $4,800 and carried for $30 a month. Today the houses built under it are selling for $23,000, with average mortgages of $18,000 against them, hopelessly beyond the reach of the ordinary person in this country. The statistics indicate that the
May 17. 1966

minimum salary to qualify for N.H.A. housing at present is $6,500 a year.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, the latest statistics show there are 7,637,000 Canadians whose income is less than the minimum necessary to qualify under the National Housing Act. What kind of housing act is that? I would have liked very much to go into the minister's analysis of the mortgage shortage and point out the basic inconsistencies in his position. He urged on us the virtues of the private enterprise system and ignored the fact that the artificial pegging of the interest rate by this government has created this situation. It is all very well to tell the builders to go and talk to the mortgage companies and tell them they should be good citizens and lend them the money under the N.H.A., and at the same time tell them they are in a free enterprise economy where the insurance companies cannot be blamed for putting their money where they realize the maximum return on it. But there is inconsistency in the whole approach the minister is taking. We should sit down in this house and take a look at the housing picture in Canada; perhaps we can do it when we have the minister's estimates before us. It is a national disgrace that from coast to coast there is no national program or development.
Our senior citizens are living under disgraceful conditions. Every member in this house has made a speech about the deplorable way we treat our senior citizens. Our great cities are rotting at the core. If I had time, I could go into the small potatoes of what has resulted from the 1964 act. I am not blaming the minister for this. He is new to the business and he is fighting the provincial and municipal governments. We can work in Ottawa for the next ten years and never really have a national housing policy, unless we do two or three things. We must have a full time minister. This is no criticism of the Minister of Labour, but he cannot do two jobs and sell a massive housing program like that. Second, we must have a new department of urban development where we could have a minister who would be able to devote his whole time and energy in an effort to co-ordinate the provinces and the municipalities in this scheme. We need some sort of conscience so that we can establish a common goal in respect of housing. I wish the minister had had a royal commission on urbanization, because then we would have had some sort of
Division
blueprint as to where we would like to take Canada. As it is, we have nothing.

subsubtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-HALIFAX DOCKYARD-FAILURE TO EFFECT WAGE PARITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the opportunity provided following the vote for members to raise particular grievances, I wonder whether I might indulge the house for a few minutes to turn to what is developing into one of the most serious labour situations in our country. I refer, Mr. Speaker, to two situations; the first concerns defence employees at H.M.C. Dockyard and its related facilities in Halifax, and the second concerns employees at H.M.C.S. Shearwater, where there are now what are commonly known as Canadian force bases.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I do not propose to detain the house in tracing the history of the formula on which the prevailing wage rate concept is based. That goes back to the late 1920's and the early 1930's. However, as other hon. members from Halifax have indicated, in the mid 1960's the basing formula for wage rates established in the 1930's is somewhat out of date.
It appears, Mr. Speaker, that legislation affecting collective bargaining will be brought before the house in the months that lie ahead. Perhaps in that legislation will be found the answers to many of the problems that I raise. However, the essence of the grievance that I raise tonight is that I do not think the government has a clear understanding of the urgency that faces not only our part of the country, but the entire nation in this regard. The employees of H.M.C. Dockyard in Halifax are adamant in their position. They strongly feel that they are entitled to a new basing formula recognizing the principle of equal pay for equal work.
I am not one of those, Mr. Speaker, who would cry danger where no danger exists. I do suggest that unless the government pays immediate attention to the problems at the dockyard, problems that affect on an over-all basis in Halifax approximately 5,000 men, those men are going to walk off their jobs. If that were to happen we shall find that our navy, army and air force based in the Nova Scotia area will be unable to function, and their operations will come to a grinding halt. Anybody who in the past has said that we do not have effective armed forces will be vindicated in that statement by the end of June
May 17, 1966

or early July unless immediate attention is paid to what these men feel are legitimate demands.
Of immediate concern for the Halifax dock workers are such matters as wage parity with their west coast equals. There are substantial differences in pay schedules between workers in the Department of National Defence dockyards on the west coast at Esquimalt and those at Halifax.
As we struggle in the Atlantic area to close the economic gap existing between ourselves and the rest of Canada, the federal authority must play its full role in helping us to achieve our goal. We cannot talk about equality of opportunity, and equal sharing in our national prosperity unless we are all prepared to do something actively and positively toward that goal. Otherwise we are paying lip service to that concept.
The concept of wage parity-to use a well worn but familiar phrase-is not new. That concept was the concern not only of this government, but of its predecessor. The government in 1961, led by the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) decided, in the case of the Department of National Defence employees in the Halifax area, that the formula governing their wages should be changed from the traditional formula governing prevailing rates. That government, as an alternative vehicle, chose a formula based on the average schedules of pay in the seven most highly paid dockyards on the Atlantic coast, including the St. Lawrence river yards. This was tantamount to a recognition by a federal authority of a national basis upon which to calculate the pay of prevailing rates for hourly paid employees.
However, when this new formula I speak of was adopted, it was generally agreed that what had been done was only an interim step. That step was designed to enable the government to arrive at a truly national formula of pay based on the averages paid in shipyards from coast to coast and on both coasts. As I say, that was an interim step. However, the government of that day had recognized the worthiness of the plea by the dockyard workers with respect to equal pay for equal work. Subsequent events have not brought about the full extension of this previous program. They have not brought about a national basis for wage rates of dockyard employees.
These employees of the federal authority remain the only group of employees who do
Labour Conditions
not enjoy national parity with respect to wages. I do not know of any other branch of service, be it the armed forces, the civil service, or any other establishment, where that condition prevails. All employees of the government except these dockyard workers, to whom our country must turn and upon whom we must keep our instruments of defence viable and actionable, enjoy national wage parity.
It is 1966 now, Mr. Speaker. It has been five years since an interim step was taken by the federal authority. Nothing further has been done. We have had lots of promises. Everybody agrees that the basing formula must be looked at with a view to changing it. So far however, nothing has been done.
Last autumn the Trades and Labour Council at H.M.C. Dockyard in Halifax presented to the government a brief in which it outlined a five year program to achieve wage parity for dockyard workers from coast to coast. This program was an orderly, well thought out and responsible map of action on their part. It showed that the program could not be carried out without consideration being taken of the effect that it would have on community businesses, doing the same repairing and overhauling as H.M.C. Dockyard, in the Halifax area. The members of the Trades and Labour Council were well aware that wages paid at the dockyard affect wages paid in similar areas of concern in the private sector of business.
May I say for the record that the formula the council proposed-it presented it to the government last fall-would have provided an opportunity for review by both the government and local interests of matter pertaining to wage parity respecting various trades within the dockyard. In no way did this brief recommend anything of an insurmountable nature. Indeed, the program set out called for the achievement of wage parity in this matter: in the first year, there would be paid 25 per cent of the difference in the schedules of wages between the west coast and east coast; in the second year, 33 per cent of the remaining difference would be paid; in the third year 50 per cent; in the fourth year, 70 per cent, and in the fifth year 100 per cent of the remaining difference would be paid.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
To say the government simply shelved the proposal and hid behind the excuse of waiting until the collective bargaining bill became an act might be oversimplification; it might,

May 17, 1966
Labour Conditions
in one sense be not entirely correct. But this does not in any way lessen the seriousness of this presentation by the employees at the dockyard and the other national defence facilities in the Dartmouth-Halifax area.
The failure of the government to act on this question of wages has brought about a situation among these highly skilled technicians-instrument makers, machinists, boilermakers-which might have been avoided. These are people skilled at trades which are vital to keeping our navy at sea and, in these days of integration, to keeping our army on wheels and our air force mobile.
In the last 12 years, in order to get a highly trained group of men into the dockyard, an apprenticeship training scheme has put 244 young men through a full course of instruction. Of these 244 people, 121 have gone elsewhere in the country to find employment simply because they found they could get more money outside the dockyard. Not all these people have left the Halifax area. They can get more money with a dozen different national companies which have established businesses in our area. This is an indication of what is happening as a result of the inability of the government to act.
I do not suggest the government must completely satisfy these men at the dockyard. They are reasonable men. They are labour men. They know there is give and take. But remember, it has cost the taxpayers of Canada more than $18,000 to train each of the apprentices I mentioned and it goes without saying that the men at the dockyard would much prefer to have had that money in their pockets than to see it go into the United States, or the west coast, or Ontario or anywhere in the private sector.
A dockyard in the eyes of many people is simply an excellent training ground for machinists, boilermakers and skilled men of all kinds. This is not why the dockyard was established. Bearing in mind the urgent necessity for wage adjustments at the dockyard before the implementation of legislation affecting collective bargaining I would ask the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) and those on the treasury benches seriously to consider a thorough review of the question of wage parity at the dockyard. I suggest the government give serious consideration to the brief submitted to them last year. These men want an answer. They do not want to be put off. They want an answer with regard to wage parity.

If the government would do this and supply the trades and labour council at the dockyard, as well as the motor transport section at Canadian Force Base Shearwater with a reasonable answer, a major step might be taken to avert what could be a most serious situation. These men have now gathered about them substantial outside support within the trades and labour council including many unions with national and international affiliations.
Each day these people are getting, union by union, more and more substantial support and confirmed intention of support through letters and other documents. I am not standing here to make a noise or to create any alarm which does not exist. I have followed the situation at the dockyard as far as it concerns this question of wages for some ten years, in spite of the fact that I am a very junior member for Halifax, and I suggest to the government that the position has never been as serious as it is at this moment.
There is a second matter on which I wish to speak. I will deal with it briefly before resuming my seat. My purpose is to outline the difficulties being experienced by the motor transport section at Canadian Force Base Shearwater. Here again the government is well aware of the difficulties faced by its employees. Not only is there disparity over the whole field of equal pay for equal work, but we also have within the region men doing exactly the same job as their counterparts two and a half miles away while being paid substantially less.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
Although the personnel at Shearwater find themselves in an identical environment, faced with similar tax rates, tax structure, merchandise costs, rental costs and construction costs as their counterparts at Dockyard in the naval armament depot, the naval magazine and other supporting facilities at the army centre, they receive an across-the-board 20 cents an hour less for their labour.
We live in an age when in our thought processes we must not overlook the dignity, value and worth of the individual. Unless we do this we are not ordained for any reasonable, Christian or otherwise, future.
I should like for a few moments to quote from certain sections of the brief prepared by the motor transport section of H.M.C.S. Shearwater on this matter. I should like first of all to put it on the record, and second, to establish in the minds of all hon. members
May 17, 1966

the urgency tor over-all consideration of the national defence employees and their plight, and the additional plight being faced by a certain group within the general complex in the Halifax area.
I quote from the brief as follows:
We would like to bring to your attention the discrimination of some of the employees in the Halifax-Dartmouth area. We are speaking of the personnel of M.T. section (H.M.C.S. Shearwater).
I notice they have not yet learned to call it the Canadian forces base.
We would like to point out the different rates of pay in this area of personnel who have the same employer (Department of National Defence). On checking with the rate scale in this area, we find the rates are as follows:
H.M.C. Dockyard	H.M.C.S. Shearwater
Driver	$2.05 Driver	$1.85
These are hourly rates in the integrated motor pool, and if these men walk out, anybody who drives a government vehicle is not going to be able to go to work in the morning. In this one category the difference is 75 cents an hour. A heavy equipment driver at Dockyard gets $2.25 an hour, and at H.M.C.S. Shearwater $2.05, 20 cents an hour less for this whole schedule of employees. Naval magazine rates are the same as Dockyard. The naval armament rates are the same as Dockyard, and also the Shannon Park rates. But Shearwater is a naval establishment. We fly airplanes from there. Although it is a naval establishment it has been classified as something less than a ship's service centre, and so the employees get 20 cents an hour less.
I would now like to give a few figures from outside the area with respect to drivers. E.M.I. Cossor pays $2.25 an hour, Imperial Oil $462 per month for a 40 hour week, which works out as $2.89 per hour, Volvo $2.05, Fairey Aviation starts at $2, and Texaco starts new men at $2 an hour.
With reference to the question of disparity of wages there is one other little group to which I should like to refer, namely employees of the marine agency of the Department of Transport in my area. They find themselves in exactly the same boat as the hourly paid employees of the Department of National Defence.
Why is it in 1966, when the government pays great lip service to the principle of equal opportunity, saying that everybody must share in the national prosperity, that these people do not obtain equality? With full awareness of what is going on at Dockyard
Labour Conditions
and the impact that this will have on our economic structure in the private sector, I simply ask the government, is it fair, is it right and is it just to continue in 1966 to avail itself of a principle and policy evolved in the late 1920's and early 1930's?
It was an effective and responsible principle through the 1930's, 1940's and perhaps through the early 1950's, but if the government wishes to say we are enjoying unprecedented prosperity, let us recognize that fact by giving consideration to the prevailing rate men at Dockyard. If the government does not give them the consideration that they deserve then, as I said at the outset of my remarks, we are going to have totally immobile Canadian forces in the Halifax area on July 1.
