However, Mr. Speaker, I am very happy that the junior member for Halifax has raised this particular matter at this time. As I started to say, he most certainly should not and need not apologize if he appears to be making a loud noise on this particular grievance. A loud noise and emphatic statement are required on this grievance because it is just as serious as he

May 17, 1966
Labour Conditions
pointed out. It is serious not only at the dockyard at Halifax but also at the dockyard at Esquimalt in B.C., where the identical situation pertains.
Year after year in this parliament the identical problem that the hon. member has spoken of has been raised, not only when the present government was in office but when the Conservative government was in office, and the only answer we received was that the matter was under consideration, and was being studied, and that something was going to be done. I know we raised this issue twice in the preceding session and that was the answer we got.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I want to add my voice to that of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Forrestall) to say that the employees at the dockyard of Esquimau feel exactly the same way as the employees at the dockyard at Halifax. They no longer are going to be satisfied with an answer to the effect that something is going to be done or that the matter is under consideration. It also is my information that if something is not done inside of 30 days, action will be taken by the men themselves and it will be an action which will be very detrimental to the maintenance and operation of our armed forces. I never have been able to understand the thinking of the government or the departments as indicated by the way they handle their wage rate policies in the dockyards of this nation. As a matter of fact their policy seems to vary from department to department, and indeed within a department itself.
In the dockyards we have a black situation. Let us take the case of the electrician. In the dockyards at Esquimau and Halifax there are two types of electricians employed; you have the inside wire men who do the construction and maintenance work, and you have the inside wire men who do the ship work. An inside wire man who works on a ship is paid at a lower rate than an inside wire man who does the construction and maintenance work on the dockyard itself.
However, under what was supposed to have been the policy, the payment should be on the basis of what is termed the prevailing rate, and the prevailing rate is the trade union rate in that locality outside the dockyard. What happens at Halifax and Esquimau? Here we have maintenance electricians on the land and the ship electricians on the ship; the ship electricians receive the

ordinary or normal rates, but in respect of the electricians in the dockyard, the Department of National Defence maintains that since they are in the dockyard they are in the same position as the inside wire men on the ship. These maintenance men never put a foot on board ship, so they cannot do any work on board ship, and yet they are cheated. They are classified at the same prevailing rate of the shipyard instead of being paid according to the poUcy which states that it shall be the prevailing rate of an inside wire man on construction and maintenance. That has been going on for years; they have been complaining for years, and still no action is taken.
There is another matter in respect of the dockyards at Halifax and Esquimau which I did not hear mentioned by the hon. member for Halifax, but it is a most intriguing and important one. At the dockyard there are many occasions when additional skilled men are required. They are brought in as extra men, as temporary but skilled men. They are brought in at the prevailing rate, the trade union rate, and are paid the full trade union rate. What happens to the permanent men who are on the job on the dockyard all the time? Because they know what has to be done and know how the job should be done, they supervise the work of these temporary men who are brought in. So you have the situation where the man who was brought in on a temporary basis is being paid at a far higher rate than the dockyard man who is supervising his work.
What kind of policy is it where you have the skilled man on the job receiving a lower rate of pay than the man he is supervising? That is the policy which has been pursued for years and which is being pursued right now at the dockyards of Halifax and Esquimau. I marvel at the patience of those thousands of employees who have put up with it for this length of time. It is no wonder they are dissatisfied; it is no wonder they have reached the limit of their patience and have reached the point where they are not going to stand for any more promises or talk. They want action or they will take action.
I have no hesitation, Mr. Speaker, in saying, from information I have received from Halifax and Esquimau, that I believe the government and the Department of National Defence right now is sitting on a powder keg and the fuse is about to be lit. You have only about 30 days and if there is no action, the government has only itself to blame.
May 17, 1966

speechtext:
The same grievance, Mr. Speaker.
I support my colleague from Halifax (Mr. Forrestall) and my colleague for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and should like to say that what they have indicated to this house, in my opinion, is pretty accurate forecast of what will happen. I think the government is sitting on a burning powder keg in connection with its prevailing rate policy in respect of the dockyards at Esquimalt and Halifax. I do not believe there is a great amount of time in which to solve the problem. Action is needed now.
I am happy to see that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) and the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) are in the chamber to hear these contributions. I would suggest they take to their government and more particularly to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson), as the minister in charge of Treasury Board, the points of view which have been expressed by the previous speakers, as well as mine. These are matters which should be dealt with quickly.
I speak particularly of the 2,400 men classified as prevailing rate employees who work in H.M.C. Dockyard. Before I go over some points in addition to those raised by my colleague, I should like to commend him for his hard work in dealing with this problem. It is not a pleasant problem to deal with. We are members of the opposition, and I suppose we could take the attitude of shrugging our shoulders and moving away from a very bad situation; but we do represent the Halifax area and we do feel we have a responsibility, if we as members of parliament are going to play any useful role at all in seeing that this situation is solved and that somehow the aspirations of these 2,400 men are met in some satisfactory way.
When my colleague and I return to our constituencies week end after week end it is not pleasant for us to see the frustrations of these men who are trying to achieve some more reasonable wage formula. So we continue to work with them. We work as a conciliatory force, and not as a force egging or urging them on. We act as a conciliatory force with the Department of National Defence in an effort to bring forth justice and
Labour Conditions
order. Nobody wishes to be a member of parliament for an area where a severe strike could break out.
No one would be proud to be a member under such circumstances, and anyone who would allow a strike or walkout to develop without an endeavour to head it off would be doing a disservice to his constituency and, since we have elements of national defence which are involved, a disservice to the whole country. My colleague has played the more active role in our dealings with this problem, but both of us have been dealing with it.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I think the points of view he has expressed here in a moderate and reasoned fashion, yet none the less with chilling overtones of what could happen if the problem is not dealt with, is an indication of his sense of responsibility, the extent of his study and his willingness to spend long hours researching into prevailing rate formulas, and factors that have to be considered by the department.
It may be suggested that collective bargaining for government employees is just around the corner and that this will provide an answer to the problems. The department or the minister may suggest that we should wait until collective bargaining is established, but I suggest that will take place too late and will only come into effect after the end of June. It will be too slow in coming and too late to deal with this particular problem. What is needed is a policy and that policy is needed now.
The Minister of National Defence, the Associate Minister and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) must realize that a policy regarding wages for non-civil servants who are classified as prevailing rate employees must be spelled out in positive terms. If there is to be collective bargaining at some future time the collective bargainers on the government side must have some policy spelled out, so they will know what to do when they sit down with the employees. The department should consider quickly a wages policy for dockyard employees so as to give at least some indication as a guideline to be applied, if not now, then when a collective bargaining team is appointed. The simple fact that collective bargaining is just around the corner is not in my opinion a sufficient answer to the situation.
My colleague has pointed out some of the factors which bedevil the Halifax situation, factors such as costs and lower wages for

May 17. 1966
Labour Conditions
dockyard employees which drive skilled workers from the area. This is something about which all Nova Scotians, maritimers and, indeed, Canadians should be vitally concerned, because these are factors which become incentives to individuals to go elsewhere, and factors of economics which cause waste and high costs in training apprentices. The cost figure in respect of training apprentices given earlier this year in answer to a question asked by my colleague was $17,000 to $18,000 per apprentice. That is taxpayers' money that is being spent. Yet many of these apprentices are going elsewhere where they can make a better living for themselves and provide more appropriately for their families. These are points that must be considered when one deals with the seriousness of the situation.
What about the formula itself? These men are classified as prevailing rate employees. In using a prevailing rate formula one looks around for comparable industries and sets wage patterns in a particular area as a result of those comparable industries. Even this procedure has its farcical aspects. As my colleague pointed out, there is a vast difference in wages paid to prevailing rate employees at the Canadian forces base at Shearwater as compared to those employed at H.M.C. Dockyard; yet men employed at both leave their places of employment to go home to adjoining houses. H.M.C. Dockyard and the base at Shearwater are very close, so there must not be a prevailing rate in existence there because of the startling wage rate differentials that exist.
A prevailing rate formula I suggest is not inappropriate for either H.M.C. Dockyard at Halifax or the station at Esquimalt. Indeed, some recognition of this fact was given by the former government in 1961 when it departed from the formula then in existence, which equated the dockyard workers with the workers at the Halifax shipyards, right next door on the Halifax waterfront, and instead adopted a formula based on an average of seven east coast yards. This represented a significant breakthrough which was achieved by the Diefenbaker government and gave heart to many maritimers, because it showed at least a glimmering of some aspect of a national wages policy, rather than a policy narrowly anchored within specific areas. This was a march in the right direction, and I suggest it is a march that should go further.

How should a wages formula be determined? I suggest that the day has long passed when dockyard workers in this country should be tied in with shipyard workers. Without denigrating the shipyard workers of this country in any way, I suggest that dockyard workers are part of today's modern sophisticated type of defence industry which relies on electronics and which is far removed from the shipyard-dockyard comparison which existed 20 years ago, near the end of the second world war.
Because of the growing sophistication in the defence industry, the dockyard industry should be treated as part of it, and if a prevailing rate formula is to be adopted, the Department of National Defence should look to other defence industries in an area to determine wage rates for dockyard workers and not look exclusively to neighbouring shipyard industries.
It must be admitted that ship construction and repair yards in Canada are not enjoying in general the economic growth which this country is enjoying. I think this is the case principally because, as a maritime nation, we are a high cost nation in competition with other countries of the world and have not fared as well as others in our shipyard industry growth.
Finally, in deciding how this formula should be considered, it is a legitimate request on the part of dockyard workers on the east coast that the government should look at wages paid to dockyard workers on the west coast as some kind of a guide as to what are proper wages. Of all industries that are comparable, surely the dockyard industry is one that falls at the top level.
In short, sir, I suggest that a national policy is needed to deal with problems raised regarding the wages paid at Esquimalt and Halifax to dockyard workers. There are legitimate grievances which are now festering in both these areas, and if these grievances are allowed to continue to fester they will erupt and break out, as forecast by the hon. members for Halifax (Mr. Forrestall) and Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). I suggest the answer is for the department to come quickly to grips with the problem in order to devise a formula which will fit the situation which exists in the mid-1960's, rather than carrying on a philosophy which was developed at some time in the mid-1920's.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
It might have been somewhat easier for my colleague and myself, from the Halifax area,
May 17. 1966

simply to let the government and the department struggle with this problem. We could have shrugged our shoulders and said, "No, we are in opposition; there is really nothing we can do to help. We cannot advance a point of view for you because no one will listen." I do not think that is a responsible attitude to take and certainly, as a member of parliament for this area, which has grievous labour problems, I do not want to take that attitude. My colleague and I are offering all the assistance we can to the government in connection with what we regard as a very difficult problem. I repeat my colleague's request and add to it my own in beseeching the government to come seriously and quickly to grips with what is a very serious problem.

I wish to point out very briefly that we are aware of the problems raised by three previous speakers and that we are now looking into them, in co-operation with the Treasury Board, the Department of Labour and the Civil Service Commission.
I know that the members who raised this matter indicated that a solution to this very difficult problem is urgently needed. I shall not give a detailed account of the various phases we went through to end up with such serious difficulties. Hon. members know as well as I do how this situation started and developed.
A review of classifications is now being made by the Civil Service Commission. That is what is imposing limitations to some extent on any possible action at the administrative level of the Department of National Defence.
Labour Conditions
Even though we are concerned with this problem and its urgency, we are restricted to a certain extent because of this reclassification undertaken by the Civil Service Commission.
Personally, every time I have had the privilege and pleasure of talking with representatives particularly from the Halifax areas, we have been able to approach the problem and exchange useful views in order to settle, temporarily at least, the most urgent matters pending the complete plan that is to be submitted by the Civil Service Commission.
As far as the two members for Halifax (Mr. Forrestall and Mr. McCleave) are concerned, I undertake, as requested by the senior member, for instance, to take up with to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) the question of whether things could not be activated. We all know that the Civil Service Commission is trying to achieve what they call occupational categories and thus set a basis for collective agreements in the various contracts that have to be renegotiated.
The date set by the Civil Service Commission is October 1, 1966. According to the hon. members, that is much to late. I am inclined to agree. There is one fact we must bear in mind: we are faced with a massive reclassification. It should be recalled that when the members of the national defence staff in particular are considering these trades -we have reduced the number as much as possible; but we still have 110-in each case they have to examine a difficult problem by itself. Speaking for myself, I have never encountered such a difficult and frustrating experience as trying to consider simultaneously 110 different problems, none of which may be considered in the abstract but each of which, as the hon. member for Halifax pointed out, involves an employee, a human being with his pride, who is entitled to some regard and to receive a decent salary for the work he is doing.
I am sure, as far as our department is concerned, that we are doing everything possible to study all these problems in the right perspective with a view to finding a fair solution. I promise the hon. members, specially the member for Halifax, and without forgetting the member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton), that I shall do everything in my power so that this salary revision is completed and we can find a solution which might not only be a rule for the present but also the key for continuity in that labour

May 17. 1966
Quebec Labour Relations classification, where social justice would remunerate equitably the employees of national defence and the other employees in the same area.
The minister has assured me that we will do everything in our power to give satisfaction to those people who have waited so long. The Civil Service Commission and the people in charge of labour relations are working on this problem which concerns us, in an endeavour to find a satisfactory solution.

Mr. Speaker, my grievance tonight deals with a situation which probably concerns the whole house, because it relates to the present strike on the St. Lawrence and the great lakes.
The regional industry of Trois-Rivieres, which I represent, is affected, and this holds true more particularly for the 500 or 600 employees directly involved; further, I do not refer to the effects from the national point of view. I believe that up to now the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) has done everything that was humanly and logically possible, by appointing the arbitration board which invited the two parties to sit Friday. I was scandalized and amazed that the management representatives refused to attend and negotiate.
I noted, like all members, that those people were invited Saturday and that the judge was asked whether he was ready to sit, because it was an urgent matter. We were hoping until Saturday afternoon, from 2.30 to 4.30 p.m., but the management representatives refused to take part in the negotiations.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think we have reached a point where we should ask the minister to take strong action and, if he lacks the powers necessary to force the management representatives to the negotiation table, I think he should ask the house for the emergency powers he needs. I have no doubt that the whole house would be pleased to give them to him, because Canada's economy as a whole is affected.
I would not want to give the impression that I have mentioned these facts for demagogic purposes; rather it is because I recall that, in 1961, when we had trouble caused by the S.I.U., when violence flared up, the employers applied to the courts for an injunction-I was mayor of the municipality and I took the necessary action to force the employees on the waterfront to comply with the
[Mr. Cadieux (Terrebonne) .1
terms of the injunction. We took strong action and forced them to comply with the law.
Then it was the employees' turn. There should not be a double standard, especially in the present case. Because of the consequences on the economy of our country, it is even more important.
I submit, and this is the suggestion I want to make on behalf of my area, knowing that there will be repercussions-I would like to ask the Minister of Labour to avail himself as soon as possible of all the authority he can dispose of to force the management representatives to negotiate. If he does not have the necessary authority, he only has to ask the house to give it to him. Afterwards, if they did not want to comply, the minister could take steps in order that navigation and transshipment of freight could continue normally.
I believe that the labour representatives, even if I do not have the authority to speak in their name, would understand, after this gesture of good will and this proof of energetic authority on the part of the minister, that it is in their interest to resume work during negotiations, because they can expect that the matter will not drag out unduly as it has dragged on since last September.

Mr. Speaker, I have a grievance different from the subjects discussed this evening. I might run five minutes past the hour in completing my grievance, so may I have your permission to do so?
I rise at this time to protest the policy now being pursued by the government in connection with naming designated areas and rewarding industry that locates and settles in these designated areas at the expense of the whole country. This policy, which is one of sheer favouritism, gives all the advantages of attracting industry to these designated areas.
I think it is also timely that I protest against this policy tonight, because at this very minute the executive and members of the Prince Edward Chamber of Commerce are meeting in Picton, Ontario, to wrestle with the problem of our failure to attract new industry. The same problem exists in Lennox as well, which has people, problems and industrial circumstances similar to those of Prince Edward.
May 17, 1966

The policies of the government are seriously impeding the economies of these two great counties. Prince Edward county has already lost a good prospective industry. The persons acting for the industry said that they could not consider locating in Prince Edward, even with all its many advantages and good qualifications, because the federal government grants were so substantial that they could not afford to pass them up.
We have in my riding, Mr. Speaker, all the responsibilities to keep our economy buoyant and rolling that are faced by the people in designated areas. We have children to educate, bills to pay, taxes to pay, taxes which are used by this government to the advantage of the designated areas and to our disadvantage. We try to promote industry but to no avail, as we cannot compete in the situation brought about by the discriminatory policies of this government. Even our students, Mr. Speaker, cannot get summer jobs because of the lack of industrial growth in the county. They go elsewhere for employment-yes, for permanent employment
I have here an article which appeared in the Picton Gazette of May 6, and I should like to quote parts of it:
Already one industry has turned down the Prince Edward area in favour of the heavy federal government assistance available in a designated area. The recommended resolution calls for Prince Edward to either be designated for industry grants or given assistance so the county can compete with designated areas.
The latter is preferable.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that industrial and economic progress can be maintained and nurtured in this country without a preferential government policy of the kind presently existing. This practice and policy of the government is creating much unrest in the nation. It is turning city against city, municipality against municipality. Who knows-as time goes by we may find that some of these federally subsidized industries have located in the wrong place and the wrong area, and may in the long run have done better to settle in the very area or areas which were turned down at the beginning. Such an area is Prince Edward-Lennox, which is splendidly located approximately half way between the two greatest metropolitan markets in Canada-I refer to Toronto and Montreal with first class rail and deep water transportation facilities, a good, vigorous, intelligent and basically capable labour pool; with living conditions and environment and recreational
Labour Conditions
conditions second to none. With these characteristics these counties can offer prospective industry the best of advantages. Existing industry now prospering in our counties is proof of this. But we cannot compete at this time with the present policies of the government, which are so partial to our neighbouring designated areas.
The Prince Edward Chamber of Commerce is working harder than ever before on industrial promotion, as is the Napanee Chamber of Commerce. But Prince Edward is getting no new industry; neither is Napanee. Both Picton and Napanee assist and encourage their existing industries all they can. The pace of present-day standards of taxation, of competition, of living, and of population growth demand that we multiply our enterprises, that we produce more in our own areas in keeping with all the circumstances pertaining to our ambitious and vigorous Canadian economy.
Prince Edward-Lennox, the Ontario home of the Loyalists and older than Canada itself, is one of the cradles of Canadian civilization. The area developed on an agricultural economy which still flourishes, despite some disadvantages. But now in 1966, Mr. Speaker, agriculture, although it can feed us, cannot keep and provide employment for us all.
That is why I call upon this government either to do away with this law delineating these designated areas, or to bend these binding restrictions on our area and make an arrangement whereby we can compete with our neighbours toward a more prosperous Canada.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: THE SENATE-SUGGESTED ACTION LEADING TO ABOLITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the orders of the day this afternoon I addressed a question to the Prime Minister with reference to a new way in which the Senate might be abolished. My question was based on a news report of the intention on the part of Premier Lesage to abolish the upper house in the province of
May 17, 1966	COMMONS
Quebec. It was on the basis of the manner in which Premier Lesage proposed to take this step that I put my question to the Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker thought that it was an improper question for the orders of the day and so I suggested that we could perhaps abolish the Senate at ten o'clock tonight.
I hope the applause is recorded in Hansard.
I think I should quote a couple of sentences attributed to Mr. Lesage in yesterday's edition of the Montreal Gazette. It is an excellent statement of the proposition that an upper, non-elected house should be abolished. These are the words from yesterday's Gazette:
Mr. Lesage said abolition is necessary to transform and democratize parliamentary procedure and put government in the hands of the people. In the future the decisions of the representative of the people must be final; they cannot be in the hands of those who are appointed.
I agree thoroughly with the sentiments expressed by Mr. Lesage, and though all members of parliament do not yet realize it-they will in due course- I believe the day has come when the affairs of our democracy should be in the hands of those who are elected by and are responsible to the people of Canada.
I raise this question, however, because I think Premier Lesage has made statements which make it necessary for this government to come forward with some comment. As hon. members are aware, in the last session of the previous parliament we were informed that the government of Quebec had asked the government of Canada to endorse a petition from the lower house of Quebec to Her Majesty the Queen for an amendment of the constitution in a manner which would curb the powers of the Quebec upper house.
I for one fully agree with Premier Lesage's aim to curb those powers or to do away with the upper house altogether. But the way in which this proposition was placed before us last session did raise some questions as to the manner in which we should amend our constitution.
Mr. Lesage has gone one step further. He has told the electors of Quebec that he now proposes to abolish the upper house in that province. He says that if his government is returned to power and if Westminster agrees to amend the British North America Act as he has requested, Quebec will then be in a position in which measures passed by the lower house cannot be vetoed by the upper house for more than a year.

So, says Mr. Lesage, the government of which he is Premier will cause to be passed a measure in the lower house abolishing the upper house. Then, if the upper house refuses to agree, a year later the lower house will pass the measure again and, ipso facto, the upper house goes.
If this is being done in Quebec on the basis of action taken by this government in Ottawa in sending the matter on to Westminster, it would suggest a course which might be taken to get rid of the upper house in the parliament of Canada. I suggest it follows. If it can be done there, in that way, in Quebec, it could be done in the same way here. We could pass a resolution in the lower house of parliament asking that the powers of the upper house be curbed so that it cannot veto a measure from this house for more than one year. Then we could ask the government, without going to the upper house for approval, to send that resolution to Westminster.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
We would thus be asking Westminster to amend our constitution. Then a year or so later, the power of the other house having been curbed, we could pass a bill in this house abolishing the other place, and a year later that would be the end of the Senate.
I want to say categorically that as a lifelong abolitionist so far as the Senate is concerned, I would not do it that way. I think it is a devious way to deal with the matter, and I would do it more directly; but this is the position that the government has helped to create. The government supported the proposition of sending a resolution from one house in Quebec to Westminster, even though the other house did not approve it.
Now we have Mr. Lesage putting everybody in a difficult position, and most of all putting Westminster in a difficult position. The tradition at Westminster is to approve without question requests for amending our constitution, and their hope is that we will not send them requests of this kind many more times. But when Westminster is told in very plain language that this present amendment of the constitution is going to be used for a purpose that was not stated when the amendment was sought, it will put the British government and the British parliament in a rather awkward position.
This was one of the reasons I asked this question this afternoon, namely that the government should be making a statement on this matter. Either the government should

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion admit that it has helped to work out a simple formula for abolishing an upper house-and if it works for Quebec it should work for this parliament-or it should take another look at what it has gone along with in sending, by executive action, approval of Mr. Lesage's request for an amendment to the B.N.A. Act, even though we in this parliament had no chance to vote for it.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that there is a bit of a mixture in the things I am talking about. I take my stand with Premier Lesage, that democracies should be run by members who are elected. There is no place for appointed upper houses, either in Quebec or here, and some day we shall be rid of them; but I do think we have to look at the niceties of constitutional procedure, and I would be interested in knowing what the comment of the government is on this very interesting development.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just heard from a member of this house who has served long and in an illustrious manner, and who has spoken many times on the form and function of parliament. But I would remind hon. members, before we talk in terms of destroying a constituent part of parliament, that there was much reason and logic to the creation of this particular institution, the Senate, by the founding fathers.
This evening I spent some time reading the address given by the then Attorney General, John A. Macdonald, on February 6, 1865, in the parliamentary debates on the subject of the confederation of the British North American provinces. One cannot read this lengthy address by this constitutional authority of the day without appreciating that many of the problems facing the colonies of those days still continue to exist in Canada.
Actually, though my experience in this house is very limited in comparison with that of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I remember vividly the year 1961 when on two occasions, in the case of class and kind legislation and in the Coyne affair, many Canadians were grateful for the existence of the other place. Sir, economic life today is governed by a mixture of private decisions taken in the corporate sector of the economy and of public decisions taken by governments, with the latter constantly assuming greater importance.
I do not think there is any argument that in the post-war years there has been a profound change in distribution of income and in economic organization, and this is to the good. But to do this soundly and well there have to be certain constitutional safeguards. It is a fact that government action brings more and more aspects of life and affairs within its orbit. Perhaps one can even say that the citizen is progressively stripped of effective influence on certain directions of government. Perhaps it is the Senate in certain particulars which becomes the great safeguard of the liberties of the public. I think of some of the persons presently holding seats in the other place whose wisdom, judgment and experience in matters of civil liberties and in matters of welfare and economic change are significant and important to the future growth and well-being of this country.
